# lgtmaybe — full documentation

> AI code review for GitHub, GitLab, Gitea, Azure DevOps, and local Git diffs. It posts inline findings and a summary on pull and merge requests, or prints findings locally. Choose from seven hosted providers, ollama, or any OpenAI-compatible endpoint. Bedrock, Vertex, and Azure support keyless cloud auth.

Source: https://lgtmaybe.coles.codes/ — generated from the docs/ tree.

---

<!-- Source: https://lgtmaybe.coles.codes/ -->

<div class="hero" markdown>

![lgtmaybe logo: a shrugging face with curly-brace arms](assets/logo.svg){ width="128" }

# lgtmaybe

</div>

lgtmaybe reviews pull and merge requests on **GitHub, GitLab, Gitea, and Azure
DevOps**. It can also review a local Git diff. Choose a hosted
model, ollama, or another OpenAI-compatible endpoint. It posts inline comments
and one summary, or prints findings locally.

It reads the diff and a little surrounding code, but comments only on changed
lines. It never checks out or runs the change. Generated files and binaries are
skipped, secrets are redacted, and all author-supplied text is treated as
untrusted.

It checks for:

- **Correctness and security:** logic errors, missed `await`s, injection, auth mistakes, and leaked secrets.
- **Code health:** performance problems, needless complexity, deprecations, and risky dependencies.
- **Tests and documentation:** missing or weak tests, stale comments, and undocumented APIs.
- **Intent:** whether the change does what its title, description, and commits say it does.
- **Ponytail:** code you don't need, and simpler or standard-library ways to do the job.
- **Architecture:** coupling, wrong-way dependencies, and broken subclass contracts that will be hard to undo.

Findings are graded `info` to `critical` and land on the changed line
they refer to. A clean change gets a 👍 **LGTM!**.

![An inline lgtmaybe review comment flagging a [CRITICAL] SQL injection vulnerability, with an explanation and a committable parameterised-query suggestion](assets/marketplace/marketplace-screenshot-1.png){ width="720" }

Slash commands can refresh a review (`/review`, `/improve`), answer a question
(`/ask`), post a structured description (`/describe`), or post
[a change overview](how-to/generate-a-change-diagram.md) (`/diagram`). The
overview rates the risk of change, lists high-impact areas, and draws a
flowchart, plus a sequence diagram when the change alters a runtime flow. Run
`lgtmaybe diagram` to print a text version locally.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    web["Storefront<br/>React<br/>places orders"]
    api["Order API<br/>Python<br/>creates orders (changed)"]
    db["Order database<br/>PostgreSQL<br/>stores orders"]
    queue["Order events<br/>SQS<br/>buffers events (new)"]
    worker["Notification worker<br/>Python<br/>sends confirmations (new)"]
    email["Email provider<br/>delivers messages"]
    web -->|calls| api
    api -->|stores in| db
    api -->|publishes to| queue
    queue -->|delivers to| worker
    worker -->|sends via| email
```

## What's New

The latest releases, built from the changelog every time the docs publish.

See the [Changelog](https://lgtmaybe.coles.codes/changelog/) for every release.

## Providers

| Provider | Auth |
|---|---|
| `openai` | `OPENAI_API_KEY` |
| `anthropic` | `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` |
| `openrouter` | `OPENROUTER_API_KEY` |
| `zai` | `ZAI_API_KEY` for GLM / Zhipu AI; optional `--api-base` for the China / coding-plan endpoint |
| `bedrock` | Ambient AWS creds via GitHub OIDC, no static key |
| `vertex` | Ambient GCP creds via Workload Identity Federation, no key |
| `azure` | Resource endpoint, plus `AZURE_API_KEY` or keyless Entra (Azure AD) creds via GitHub OIDC |
| `ollama` | None: local only, zero cost |
| `openai-compatible` | `--api-base` to any OpenAI `/v1` endpoint; key optional (placeholder for keyless local servers) |

## Where It Posts

The model provider and the code host are independent: any provider above works
on any host below.

| Host | How it runs | Token | Guide |
|---|---|---|---|
| GitHub | GitHub Action | `GITHUB_TOKEN` | [GitHub Action](how-to/use-as-github-action.md) |
| GitLab | GitLab CI job | `GITLAB_TOKEN` | [Review on GitLab](how-to/review-on-gitlab.md) |
| Gitea | Gitea Actions | `GITEA_TOKEN` | [Review on Gitea](how-to/review-on-gitea.md) |
| Azure DevOps | Azure Pipelines job | `SYSTEM_ACCESSTOKEN` or `AZURE_DEVOPS_TOKEN` | [Review on Azure DevOps](how-to/review-on-azure-devops.md) |
| None | `lgtmaybe review` locally | n/a | [Install the CLI](how-to/install-the-cli.md) |

The same review runs on every host. They differ in thread resolution,
incremental reviews, and keyless cloud auth. See
[Architecture](explanation/architecture.md#code-hosts-forges) for the details.

## For AI Agents

The site root publishes a curated [`llms.txt`](llms.txt) index of these docs,
plus a whole-corpus [`llms-full.txt`](llms-full.txt), for LLM crawlers and
coding agents.

# Getting Started with lgtmaybe

This tutorial walks you through your first review using **ollama**, which runs
the model on your own machine, costs nothing, and needs no API keys. By the end
you will have reviewed a branch and seen the findings in your terminal, with no
GitHub token and no pull request.

## What You Need

- Python 3.11 or later
- [ollama](https://ollama.com) running locally
- A local git repository with some changes on a branch to review

## Step 1: Install lgtmaybe

```bash
pip install lgtmaybe
```

On macOS you can install from the Homebrew tap instead:

```bash
brew tap MattJColes/tap
brew trust MattJColes/tap   # current Homebrew requires trusting third-party taps
brew install lgtmaybe
```

[Install the CLI](../how-to/install-the-cli.md) explains the `brew trust` step,
the Windows (WinGet) install, and which providers the base install covers.
API-key and local providers work out of the box; keyless cloud providers need a
`pip` extra.

Verify the install:

```bash
lgtmaybe --help
```

## Step 2: Start ollama and Pull a Model

```bash
ollama serve          # starts the local server on http://localhost:11434
ollama pull qwen3.6:27b   # or any model you prefer
```

Leave `ollama serve` running in a separate terminal.

## Step 3: Point lgtmaybe at ollama

lgtmaybe has no built-in model, so tell it once which provider and model to
use:

```bash
lgtmaybe config init
```

It finds the running ollama and the models you have pulled, so you only
confirm:

```console
Found ollama running at http://localhost:11434 (1 model pulled) - use ollama? [Y/n]:
Pulled models: qwen3.6:27b
Model [qwen3.6:27b]:
Checking ollama / qwen3.6:27b with one short request...
OK: the model answered.
Wrote /home/you/.config/lgtmaybe/config.yml
Next: lgtmaybe review
```

Press Enter twice. Before it writes anything, it sends the model one tiny
request, so a stopped server or a model you have not pulled fails here, not
halfway through a review. The file holds only the provider and model; if you
later use a hosted provider, its API key stays in your environment.

If ollama is on another machine, answer `n`, choose `ollama`, and enter its
address. You can also skip `config init` and pass `--provider ollama --model
qwen3.6:27b` to each command. Without either, `lgtmaybe review` stops straight
away and tells you to run `config init`.

## Step 4: Review Your Changes

From inside a git repo, on a branch with some changes, run:

```bash
lgtmaybe review
```

lgtmaybe diffs your current branch against the remote primary branch
(`origin/HEAD`, falling back to `origin/main` / `origin/master`, then a local
`main` / `master`). It sends the diff, with some surrounding lines for context,
to your local qwen3.6:27b model and prints the findings to your terminal:

```console
src/app.py:14  [MEDIUM] Missing None check before use (confidence 8/10)
  find_user() returns None for an unknown id, so user.email raises AttributeError.

1 finding · risk low (no risk signals) · provider ollama · model qwen3.6:27b · lgtmaybe 2.11.1
```

Each finding shows its file and line, severity, and title, then the
explanation. The last line counts the findings, rates the risk of the change,
and names the model and lgtmaybe version.

To review the whole worktree (your branch's commits plus uncommitted edits),
add `--working`. To review only the uncommitted edits, add `--uncommitted`. To
diff against a different base, pass `--base main`.

`lgtmaybe review --help` lists the everyday options; `--help-all` adds the
advanced tuning ones.

## Step 5: Change the Output Format

`--format` controls what `review` prints. `--json` (shorthand for
`--format json`) emits a JSON array ready to pipe into other tooling:

```bash
lgtmaybe review --json
```

`--format agent` prints the findings as correction instructions an AI coding
agent can read and apply, for a local review-and-fix loop. See
[Fix findings with an AI agent](../how-to/fix-findings-with-an-ai-agent.md).

`--format sarif` prints a SARIF 2.1.0 log you can upload to GitHub code
scanning or open in an IDE. See
[Upload findings as SARIF](../how-to/upload-findings-as-sarif.md).

## Step 6: See the Whole Change

`lgtmaybe diagram` sends the same local diff to three concurrent model calls and
prints the **change overview**:

- a description of what you changed
- a risk-of-change rating (computed locally, no model call)
- a **High Impact Areas** section calling out anything that could bite, such as
  infrastructure, security posture, outage risk, migrations, or backups
- a diagram of the components your change touches, plus a sequence diagram
  when it alters a run-time flow

```bash
lgtmaybe diagram
```

It takes the same `--base` / `--working` / `--uncommitted` flags as `review`.
Run `review` then `diagram` before you open a pull request: the first tells you
what's wrong with the change, the second what the change is and what it could
break. The diagrams print as Mermaid source plus a text rendering for the
terminal. Paste the Mermaid into a GitHub comment or
[mermaid.live](https://mermaid.live) to see it drawn. See
[Generate a change overview](../how-to/generate-a-change-diagram.md).

## Step 7: Post Reviews on Real Pull Requests

The CLI reviews local changes. To post inline comments and a summary on real
pull requests, wire lgtmaybe into your code host. The review is the same on
every host; only the setup differs:

- **GitHub:** add the Action to your repo.
  See [Use as a GitHub Action](../how-to/use-as-github-action.md).
- **GitLab:** add a CI job.
  See [Review on GitLab](../how-to/review-on-gitlab.md).
- **Gitea:** add a Gitea Actions workflow.
  See [Review on Gitea](../how-to/review-on-gitea.md).
- **Azure DevOps:** add an Azure Pipelines build validation policy.
  See [Review on Azure DevOps](../how-to/review-on-azure-devops.md).

## What Happened Under the Hood

lgtmaybe ran its pipeline over your local diff:

1. **Fetch:** read the diff from your local repo with `git`.
2. **Filter:** skipped generated files, binaries, and lockfiles, and redacted
   anything that looked like a secret.
3. **Review:** sent four concurrent model calls (security, correctness, code
   health, and artefacts for tests and documentation), each asking for findings
   as JSON.
4. **Parse and anchor:** validated each reply against the findings schema and
   pinned every finding to the changed line it quotes.
5. **Reflect:** asked the model to audit its own findings and dropped the ones
   it could not stand behind.
6. **Filter findings:** dropped defect findings with no concrete failure
   scenario and anything below the severity floor (`low` by default).
7. **Render:** printed the findings. The GitHub Action posts them to the pull
   request instead.

## Next Steps

- To configure severity thresholds, path filters, and token caps, see
  [Configure .lgtmaybe.yml](../how-to/configure-lgtmaybe-yml.md).
- To use a cloud provider with no API keys, see
  [Review with Bedrock OIDC](../how-to/review-with-bedrock-oidc.md) or
  [Review with Vertex WIF](../how-to/review-with-vertex-wif.md).
- To use lgtmaybe in a GitHub Actions workflow, see
  [Use as a GitHub Action](../how-to/use-as-github-action.md).

# Install the CLI

Install the `lgtmaybe` command-line tool once, then point it at any provider.
This page covers getting the CLI onto your machine. Choosing a model backend (a
hosted API, keyless cloud, or a local model) comes after: see the
[provider how-tos](../index.md#providers) and
[Choose a review model](choose-a-review-model.md).

## Install (pip)

Works on any OS with Python 3.11+:

```bash
pip install lgtmaybe
```

Verify it:

```bash
lgtmaybe --help
```

That prints the command list with usage examples. `<command> --help` lists a
command's options. For `lgtmaybe review` it shows only the everyday ones and
ends with a line pointing at `lgtmaybe review --help-all`, which lists the
advanced tuning options too.

To check which build you are running, for a bug report or a benchmark record:

```bash
lgtmaybe --version
```

It prints one line, `lgtmaybe <version>`, for every install method (pip,
Homebrew, or the Windows executable). A source checkout that was never
installed has no version metadata and prints `lgtmaybe unknown`.

Upgrade later with `pip install --upgrade lgtmaybe`.

## Install on Windows (WinGet)

The WinGet package is a portable executable for Windows x86_64 (64-bit).
Install it by its exact package identifier:

```powershell
winget install --id MattJColes.lgtmaybe --exact
```

Verify the command alias:

```powershell
lgtmaybe --help
```

Upgrade or uninstall it later with the same package identifier:

```powershell
winget upgrade --id MattJColes.lgtmaybe --exact
winget uninstall --id MattJColes.lgtmaybe --exact
```

If WinGet cannot find a newly published version, refresh its package sources
and retry:

```powershell
winget source update
```

The executable bundles ast-grep for cross-file symbol resolution. It does not
bundle the optional cloud SDKs for keyless Bedrock, Vertex, or Azure, so use
pip with the matching extra for those providers (see
[below](#cloud-providers-need-extras)). `pip install lgtmaybe` also works on
Windows.

## Install on macOS (Homebrew)

On macOS (and Linuxbrew) you can install from the project's
[Homebrew tap](https://github.com/MattJColes/homebrew-tap) instead of `pip`:

```bash
brew tap MattJColes/tap
brew trust MattJColes/tap
brew install lgtmaybe
```

The middle step is required. Current Homebrew refuses to load a formula from a
third-party tap until you explicitly **trust** it (`Error: Refusing to load
formula … from untrusted tap`). You decide this once per machine, for every tap
outside Homebrew's core, and a tap author cannot waive it for you. To trust
only this formula instead of the whole tap, use
`brew trust --formula MattJColes/tap/lgtmaybe`.

`brew install MattJColes/tap/lgtmaybe` taps and installs in one line, but still
needs the `brew trust` step first or it stops at the untrusted-tap error.

Upgrade later with `brew upgrade lgtmaybe`.

If you tapped the earlier `MattJColes/lgtmaybe` name, switch over once with
`brew untap MattJColes/lgtmaybe && brew tap MattJColes/tap`, then
`brew trust MattJColes/tap`. Upgrades keep working on the old tap because GitHub
redirects the renamed repo, so switching is optional tidying.

Homebrew installs lgtmaybe into its own virtualenv, so it never touches your
system or project Python. The formula installs lgtmaybe and its dependencies
from prebuilt **PyPI wheels** (no compiling), so a first install takes about a
minute, mostly download time. There is no prebuilt bottle, so it works on any
architecture and macOS version. It also installs the `ast-grep` formula, which
lgtmaybe uses for cross-file symbol resolution.

## Cloud Providers Need Extras

The base pip install, Homebrew formula, and Windows executable cover every
API-key and local provider:

| Providers | Covered by base install? |
|---|---|
| `openai`, `anthropic`, `openrouter`, `zai`: set the provider's API key in your environment | ✅ Yes |
| `ollama`, `openai-compatible`: point `--api-base` at the server (local, or a hosted OpenAI-compatible API) | ✅ Yes |
| `bedrock`, `vertex`, `azure`: keyless cloud (OIDC/WIF) | ❌ Needs an extra |

The keyless cloud providers need cloud SDKs that the Homebrew formula and
Windows executable do not bundle. Install the CLI from PyPI with the matching
extra:

```bash
pip install 'lgtmaybe[bedrock]'   # or [vertex] / [azure]
```

Or run them through the [GitHub Action](use-as-github-action.md), whose image
bundles all three SDKs and handles the OIDC/WIF exchange for you.

To use `--static-analysis` locally, install the tools it drives with
`pip install 'lgtmaybe[static-analysis]'` (ruff, bandit, mypy, semgrep, and
zizmor). gitleaks and osv-scanner are separate binaries you install yourself;
any tool that is not installed is skipped. The Action image bundles all of
them.

To serve reviews to a coding agent with `lgtmaybe mcp`, install the MCP SDK
with `pip install 'lgtmaybe[mcp]'`. The Homebrew formula and Windows executable
do not include it. See
[Use from a coding agent over MCP](use-from-a-coding-agent-over-mcp.md).

## Configure a Provider

lgtmaybe has no built-in model, so tell it which provider and model to use
once:

```bash
lgtmaybe config init
```

It looks for a provider API key in your environment (`ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`,
`OPENAI_API_KEY`, `OPENROUTER_API_KEY`, `ZAI_API_KEY`), Azure, AWS or Google
Cloud credentials, and a running ollama with its pulled models. It offers the
first one it finds, suggests a current model, then checks the pair with one
tiny request so a wrong key or model fails now rather than mid-review. It
writes the provider and model to `~/.config/lgtmaybe/config.yml`; API keys stay
in your environment and are never written. Pass `--no-verify` to skip the
check, for example when you are offline.

Until a provider is configured (by `config init`, a `.lgtmaybe.yml`, or
`--provider`/`--model`), `lgtmaybe review` stops at once with a pointer to
`config init` instead of guessing a model.

## Next Steps

- Run your first local review: [Getting started](../tutorial/getting-started.md).
- Diagram what a change touches: [Generate a change overview](generate-a-change-diagram.md).
- Post reviews on real pull requests: [Use as a GitHub Action](use-as-github-action.md).

# Choose a Review Model

**Start with `google/gemini-3.8-flash` on OpenRouter.** In the 24 September
2026 benchmark on lgtmaybe 2.8.5, it led the 11 tested models on both small,
varied changes (60.9%) and large Python diffs (71.4%), and its breadth result
is fully adjudicated. It still flagged findings on seven of nine clean changes,
so check its output before acting on it.

```bash
export OPENROUTER_API_KEY=...
lgtmaybe review --provider openrouter --model google/gemini-3.8-flash
```

If large diffs matter more than small changes, consider `openai/gpt-6-luna`. It
was second on long horizon (64.6%) and finished those five cases in 440 seconds
of total review time, against Gemini's 798. Its breadth recall was much lower
(42.9% against 62.9%), so it is not the everyday default.

These recommendations come from a synthetic corpus, not your repository. Try
the candidates on recent pull requests before choosing a team default. See [Review with OpenRouter](review-with-openrouter.md) for setup.

## What the Suites Measure

- **Breadth:** 32 small changes across seven programming languages, GitHub
  Actions, and Terraform, with 72 planted findings and nine verified-clean
  changes. Each model reviews the suite three times; the table reports the
  median result.
- **Long horizon:** Four increasingly large Python changes with eight planted
  bugs each, plus one large clean change. Each model reviews the suite once.

The suites use different cases, so **compare scores within a suite, never
across suites.** Score is closed-world F0.5, which weights precision above
recall, multiplied by completeness: the share of review calls that returned
parseable findings. An unmatched finding counts as a false positive even if it
might be useful on real code. A provisional breadth score still has a few
findings awaiting human adjudication.

## Cloud Models Tested on lgtmaybe 2.8.5

### Small Changes: Breadth

| Model | Score | Recall | Precision | False positives | Clean pass |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| `google/gemini-3.8-flash` | **60.9%** | 62.9% | 79.3% | 12 | 22.2% |
| `x-ai/grok-4.7` † | 55.7% | 62.9% | 70.1% | 20 | 11.1% |
| `z-ai/glm-5.3-flash` † | 55.1% | 62.9% | 70.0% | 21 | 11.1% |
| `moonshotai/kimi-k3` † | 52.0% | 65.7% | 63.3% | 27 | 0.0% |
| `openai/gpt-6-sol` | 50.0% | 60.0% | 62.9% | 26 | 11.1% |
| `openai/gpt-6-luna` † | 50.0% | 42.9% | 70.5% | 13 | 22.2% |
| `z-ai/glm-5.3` † | 49.9% | 64.3% | 67.6% | 22 | 11.1% |
| `xiaomi/mimo-v2.6-flash` † | 46.2% | 62.9% | 61.3% | 29 | 0.0% |
| `qwen/qwen3.8-flash` † | 45.4% | 62.9% | 59.5% | 32 | 11.1% |
| `openai/gpt-6-astra` | 27.7% | 44.3% | 66.7% | 16 | 44.4% |
| `anthropic/claude-opus-5.5` | 6.0% | 1.4% | 100.0% | 0 | 100.0% |

† Provisional: some borderline findings remain unadjudicated. Clean pass is
the share of nine clean changes on which the model returned no findings. Opus's
perfect precision and clean pass came from finding almost none of the planted
bugs. Astra's score was limited in part by 45.3% completeness.

### Large Diffs: Long Horizon

| Model | Score | Recall | Precision | False positives |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| `google/gemini-3.8-flash` | **71.4%** | 87.5% | 75.7% | 9 |
| `openai/gpt-6-luna` | 64.6% | 84.4% | 69.2% | 12 |
| `openai/gpt-6-sol` | 30.6% | 78.1% | 29.8% | 59 |
| `moonshotai/kimi-k3` | 30.4% | 100.0% | 37.6% | 53 |
| `qwen/qwen3.8-flash` | 28.3% | 78.1% | 58.1% | 18 |
| `openai/gpt-6-astra` | 25.5% | 56.2% | 40.0% | 27 |
| `z-ai/glm-5.3-flash` | 24.3% | 59.4% | 48.7% | 20 |
| `x-ai/grok-4.7` | 21.9% | 65.6% | 36.2% | 37 |
| `xiaomi/mimo-v2.6-flash` | 21.5% | 71.9% | 44.2% | 29 |
| `z-ai/glm-5.3` | 8.1% | 81.2% | 12.4% | 183 |
| `anthropic/claude-opus-5.5` | 0.0% | 0.0% | 100.0% | 0 |

Kimi found all 32 planted bugs but added 53 false positives. The low scores
for Qwen Flash and Xiaomi also reflect completeness below 50%: many of their
review calls produced no parseable findings. The [benchmark results][results] show
per-case recall, token use, truncation, and wall time.

## Local Models

The published local runs used older lgtmaybe versions and have not been
repeated on 2.8.5. Among local models with canonical runs on both suites,
`nvidia/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-NVFP4` is the strongest: 48.2% breadth on 2.2.0 and
43.8% long horizon on 2.1.4. Treat those numbers as a starting point for a
local trial, not a comparison with the cloud tables above. The example below
reaches it through a local OpenAI-compatible server such as vLLM:

```bash
lgtmaybe review \
  --provider openai-compatible \
  --model nvidia/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-NVFP4 \
  --api-base http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1
```

See [Run locally with ollama](run-locally-with-ollama.md) for hardware guidance
and [Other OpenAI-compatible servers](use-a-custom-openai-compatible-endpoint.md)
for vLLM, llama.cpp, and LM Studio setup.

## Source and Limits

The [benchmark repository][bench] holds the live leaderboard, [complete
results][results], reproducible commands, and append-only raw results. Older
runs stay there for historical comparison, but their model versions, lgtmaybe
versions, and sometimes review profiles differ. The cloud recommendations on
this page use the 22 canonical runs from 24 September 2026 (11 models, two
suites).

The corpus is synthetic and does not measure provider price, availability,
data handling, or performance on your codebase. No run in this cohort has an
immutable audit trace; the live leaderboard reports audit availability.

[bench]: https://github.com/MattJColes/lgtmaybe-benchmarks
[results]: https://github.com/MattJColes/lgtmaybe-benchmarks/blob/main/RESULTS.md

# Use lgtmaybe as a GitHub Action

Use this guide to add lgtmaybe to a repository as a GitHub Actions workflow
that reviews pull requests automatically.

!!! tip "Not on GitHub?"

    lgtmaybe runs the same review on GitLab and Gitea. See
    [Review on GitLab](./review-on-gitlab.md) or
    [Review on Gitea](./review-on-gitea.md).

lgtmaybe is listed on the
[GitHub Marketplace](https://github.com/marketplace/actions/lgtmaybe). It is a
**GitHub Action**: the reviewer runs in your workflow, and its provider, model,
and provider credentials go in the step's `with:` block. Reviews post as
`github-actions[bot]` using the workflow's own token. To post as
`lgtmaybe[bot]` instead, install the public lgtmaybe App and set
`github_identity: lgtmaybe`; the App changes only the comment author. The
[minimal OpenAI workflow](#minimal-workflow-openai) below shows the complete
default setup, and
[`examples/workflows/`](https://github.com/MattJColes/lgtmaybe/tree/main/examples/workflows)
has a ready-to-copy workflow for every cloud and API-key provider.

Alongside the review, lgtmaybe posts a change overview comment on opened,
reopened, and pushed-to pull requests (`auto_diagram`, on by default). It
holds a description, a risk-of-change rating, a **High Impact Areas** section,
and a Mermaid flowchart, plus a sequence diagram when the change alters a
run-time flow. Each push refreshes it. Set `auto_diagram: false` for no
overview, or drop one section with `auto_describe: false`, `high_impact: false`,
or `risk: false`. If the PR description, or a comment lgtmaybe didn't post,
already has a Mermaid diagram, the automatic overview is skipped and the review
summary says so. `/diagram` still posts one on request.

ollama runs the model on your own machine, so use it through the
[CLI](run-locally-with-ollama.md) rather than a posting workflow.

- [Security requirement: pull_request_target](#security-requirement-pull_request_target)
- [Who can trigger a review](#who-can-trigger-a-review)

- [Choose the GitHub author](#choose-the-github-author)
- [Other key-based providers](#other-key-based-providers)
- [Keyless cloud workflows](#keyless-cloud-workflows)
- [Action inputs](#action-inputs)
