- [Adding a config file](#adding-a-config-file)
- [Pin to a specific version](#pin-to-a-specific-version)
- [On another code host](#on-another-code-host)

## Security Requirement: pull_request_target

All lgtmaybe workflows use the `pull_request_target` trigger, not
`pull_request`. This is non-negotiable:

- `pull_request_target` runs in the context of the **base branch**, so it can
  read secrets and write to the PR.
- lgtmaybe **never checks out or runs PR code**. It fetches the diff through
  the GitHub API, so the PR author cannot get code to run in the reviewer's
  environment.

The action reads the PR from the triggering event, so there is no PR URL input
to set. On an `issue_comment` event it runs the slash command (`/review`,
`/improve`, `/ask`, `/describe`, `/diagram`) through the same engine. On a
`synchronize` push the review is **incremental** by default: only the commits
added since the last completed review are reviewed, and earlier findings stay
open until fixed. Comment `/review full` for a full re-review, or fix the
behaviour with the `incremental` input or config key.

Replies inside finding threads do not trigger lgtmaybe, and a reply is not
evidence that a finding is fixed. Push the fix instead: when the next review no
longer reports the finding and GitHub marks the thread outdated, lgtmaybe
resolves the thread and replies `✅ Looks resolved.` Use `/ask` when you want
the model to answer a question.

> **Upgrading:** the `answer_replies` option has been removed. Delete it from
> `.lgtmaybe.yml` (configuration is strict, so a leftover key is an error) and
> from your Action inputs, and remove the `pull_request_review_comment` trigger
> from custom workflows.

> **Note on cost.** With ollama the model runs on your own hardware, so reviews
> are free. On a hosted provider each run uses tokens you pay for, so decide
> who can trigger one (next section). The default limits that to people you
> trust, and `max_files` (in `.lgtmaybe.yml`) and `max_input_tokens` keep any
> single run modest.

## Who Can Trigger a Review

You choose who reviews run for. The example workflows gate the `review` job on
the triggering user's
[author association](https://docs.github.com/en/graphql/reference/enums#commentauthorassociation)
and default to **trusted contributors**: `OWNER`, `MEMBER`, and `COLLABORATOR`.
A maintainer can still review an outside contributor's PR at any time by
commenting `/review` on it, because their own association passes the gate.

The same `if:` also requires a comment to carry a slash command before any job
starts. `issue_comment` fires on every comment on every pull request, so
without that clause an ordinary "lgtm, merging" would claim a runner, pull the
container, and start Python only to find no command and exit. That spends no
tokens, but it queues a job ahead of reviews that have work to do. The check is
substring-based and case-insensitive, so `/REVIEW` and `/review full` both pass.

To change the policy, edit the `if:` on the `review` job:

- **Everyone:** drop the author-association checks so any PR or slash command
  runs a review (keep the slash-command clause, or every comment starts a job).
  This suits an open project, but on a hosted provider it means anyone can
  start a paid run.
- **Returning contributors too:** add `CONTRIBUTOR` to also auto-review anyone
  who has committed to the repository before.
- **Admins only:** keep just `OWNER` (plus `MEMBER` for your organisation).

For extra guardrails, require approval for fork-PR workflow runs in
**Settings → Actions → General → Fork pull request workflows**, or move the
provider key behind a protected `environment`. See
[Trust and Cost](../explanation/trust-and-cost.md) for the reasoning behind
these options.

## Minimal Workflow: openai

```yaml
name: lgtmaybe

on:
  pull_request_target:
  issue_comment:
    types: [created]

permissions:
  contents: read
  pull-requests: write

# One run per PR and event type: a new push cancels an in-flight review, but
# the overview's own issue_comment event cannot cancel the review that posted it.
concurrency:
  group: lgtmaybe-${{ github.event.pull_request.number || github.event.issue.number }}-${{ github.event_name }}
  cancel-in-progress: true

jobs:
  review:
    # Only trusted authors (owner / member / collaborator) can trigger a review,
    # and a comment only starts a job when it carries a slash command.
    if: >-
      (github.event_name == 'pull_request_target' &&
       contains(fromJson('["OWNER", "MEMBER", "COLLABORATOR"]'), github.event.pull_request.author_association)) ||
      (github.event.issue.pull_request &&
       contains(fromJson('["OWNER", "MEMBER", "COLLABORATOR"]'), github.event.comment.author_association) &&
       (contains(github.event.comment.body, '/review') ||
        contains(github.event.comment.body, '/improve') ||
        contains(github.event.comment.body, '/ask') ||
        contains(github.event.comment.body, '/describe') ||
        contains(github.event.comment.body, '/diagram')))
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7 # base repo only, for .lgtmaybe.yml
      - uses: MattJColes/lgtmaybe@v2
        with:
          provider: openai
          model: gpt-5.5
          api_key: ${{ secrets.OPENAI_API_KEY }}
```

## Choose the GitHub Author

The minimal workflow uses GitHub's built-in workflow token and posts as
`github-actions[bot]`. This is the default and needs no App installation.

To post as `lgtmaybe[bot]`, install the public lgtmaybe App on selected
repositories, add `id-token: write` to the workflow, and set
`github_identity: lgtmaybe`. The provider, model, and provider key stay where
they are. [Post as lgtmaybe[bot]](./post-as-a-github-app.md) has the complete
workflow, the permission boundary, and uninstall instructions.

If your organisation runs its own GitHub App, the same guide covers the
advanced `app_id` / `app_private_key` inputs.

## Other Key-Based Providers

Swap the `provider`, `model`, and `api_key` inputs:

```yaml
# anthropic
- uses: MattJColes/lgtmaybe@v2
  with:
    provider: anthropic
    model: claude-sonnet-4-6
    api_key: ${{ secrets.ANTHROPIC_API_KEY }}

# openrouter
- uses: MattJColes/lgtmaybe@v2
  with:
    provider: openrouter
    model: anthropic/claude-sonnet-4.6
    api_key: ${{ secrets.OPENROUTER_API_KEY }}

# zai (GLM / Zhipu AI)
- uses: MattJColes/lgtmaybe@v2
  with:
    provider: zai
    model: glm-4.6
    api_key: ${{ secrets.ZAI_API_KEY }}

# openai-compatible (here DeepSeek's hosted API)
- uses: MattJColes/lgtmaybe@v2
  with:
    provider: openai-compatible
    model: deepseek-chat
    api_base: https://api.deepseek.com/v1
    api_key: ${{ secrets.OPENAI_COMPATIBLE_API_KEY }}
```

For each one, create an API key in the provider's console, add it as a
repository secret (**Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions**), and
reference it as `api_key`.

## Keyless Cloud Workflows

Bedrock (AWS OIDC), Vertex (GCP WIF), and Azure (Entra OIDC) need **no API keys
in secrets**. Pass `aws_role_arn`, `gcp_wif_provider`, or `azure_client_id` and
the action performs the keyless token exchange for you. All three need the
`id-token: write` permission. See:

- [Review with Bedrock OIDC](./review-with-bedrock-oidc.md)
- [Review with Vertex WIF](./review-with-vertex-wif.md)
- [Review with Azure OpenAI](./review-with-azure.md)

## Action Inputs

Every input is optional. Leave one empty to use the default shown. Most review
settings can also go in `.lgtmaybe.yml`; an input you set overrides the file.

### Provider and Model

| Input | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `provider` | none | One of `openai`, `openrouter`, `anthropic`, `zai`, `bedrock`, `vertex`, `azure`, `ollama`, `openai-compatible` |
| `model` | none | Model identifier for the chosen provider |
| `api_key` | none | API key for key-based providers, including hosted `openai-compatible` endpoints. Leave empty for bedrock, vertex, ollama, keyless azure, and keyless local servers |
| `api_base` | none | Resource endpoint for azure (`https://<resource>.openai.azure.com`), the `/v1` base for `openai-compatible` (for example `https://api.deepseek.com/v1`), or a custom base URL for another provider |
| `fallback_model` | none | Model to re-run a call on when `model` cannot answer it. For a truncated reply it is the *last* remedy, tried only after a smaller payload, a lower `reasoning_effort`, and reasoning switched off have failed on `model`; for any other failure lgtmaybe switches to it straight away. Overrides `fallback_model` in `.lgtmaybe.yml`. See [Configure fallback_model](configure-lgtmaybe-yml.md#fallback_model) for provider scope, cost, and failure behaviour |
| `triage_model` | none (no triage) | Cheap model that runs first to skip plainly non-substantive files and rank the rest by risk. Security-relevant files always escalate past triage |
| `reflect_model` | `model` | Model for the self-reflection (false-positive audit) pass. Point it at a stronger model to audit a weaker reviewer's findings |
| `language` | English | Human language for finding titles and bodies and the describe/diagram text (for example `Japanese`). Paths, severities, and suggested code are unchanged |

### What Runs

| Input | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `preset` | `fast` | `fast` runs five calls (security, correctness, code health, artefacts for tests and documentation, and architecture) on every provider; `full` runs one call per lens. An explicit `categories` list in `.lgtmaybe.yml` overrides it |
| `incremental` | auto | Review only the commits added since the last completed review on `synchronize` pushes, and the whole PR elsewhere. `true`/`false` forces it. Falls back to a full review after a force-push or when there is no earlier review. `/review full` forces a full re-review on demand |
| `recursive` | `true` | Review a file whose diff exceeds `max_input_tokens` hunk by hunk instead of sending it whole. Set `false` to disable |
| `spec_review` | `true` | Check the diff against a committed spec (OpenSpec, GitHub Spec Kit, Kiro). Runs only when a spec is detected and matches the PR, so a repository without specs pays nothing |
| `static_analysis` | `false` | Run deterministic tools (ruff, bandit, mypy, gitleaks, zizmor, ast-grep, osv-scanner, semgrep) in a sandbox over the changed files. Linters feed the model untrusted hints to confirm or discard; gitleaks, zizmor, ast-grep, and osv-scanner post findings directly with no model call. The image bundles every tool and an offline vulnerability database |
| `mid_review_retrieval` | `false` | Let a lens ask once for read-only files outside the diff, then re-run with them, instead of hedging a cross-file finding. Costs at most one extra call per batch and lens |
| `symbol_resolution` | `true` | During reflection, use ast-grep in a read-only shallow clone of the base branch to find the definition of a symbol a finding depends on, so cross-file findings are re-judged against the real code |
| `learn_feedback` | `true` | On a re-run, suppress a finding a human reacted 👎 to on its inline comment. Resolving a thread is not a suppress signal (it means fixed) |
| `resolve_fixed` | `true` | Resolve a finding's conversation once a re-run no longer reports it and the thread is outdated. Set `false` to resolve by hand |

### What Gets Posted

| Input | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `auto_diagram` | `true` | On an opened, reopened, or pushed-to PR, post or refresh the change overview comment. Set `false` to opt out of the whole comment |
| `auto_describe` | `true` | Head the change overview with a structured description (title, change type, summary, per-file walkthrough, intent check). Set `false` to drop the section; `/describe` still works |
| `high_impact` | `true` | Include the High Impact Areas section: infrastructure, security posture, outage risk, data migrations, backups and recovery, compatibility, observability, dependencies, cost, and compliance. Set `false` to drop the section and its model call |
| `risk` | `true` | Rate the PR's risk of change (low/medium/high/critical) from importer counts, sensitive paths, size, and untested code. Deterministic, no model call. Shown on the summary line, in the overview, as a hidden `lgtmaybe-risk` marker, and (with `pr_labels`) as a `risk/<level>` label |
| `pr_labels` | `false` | Attach derived labels: `review-effort/1-5`, `possible-security-issue`, `consider-splitting`, and `risk/<level>`. Best-effort, no extra model calls |
| `fail_on` | off | Merge-gate threshold (`info`/`low`/`medium`/`high`/`critical`). Creates a `lgtmaybe` Check Run that **fails** when any finding is at or above this severity. See [Gate merges on findings](#gate-merges-on-findings) |
| `profile` | `false` | Print a timing profile in the Action log: per-stage and per-call tables with token and prompt-cache usage |

### Limits and Model Tuning

| Input | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `timeout` | provider default (ollama/openai-compatible/openrouter 1800s, cloud 600s) | Enforced wall-clock timeout for each model call. For ollama and openai-compatible, which may be a single-slot server that queues calls, the default is multiplied by the concurrency, then capped at `max_review_seconds` but never below 1800s. Transient failures (capacity 429s, connection blips, 5xx) are retried with exponential backoff; permanent ones (bad key, quota or billing 429, unknown model) and a call that uses up this whole timeout fail fast, because re-sending the same request against the same budget would only burn it twice |
| `max_review_seconds` | `3600` | Soft wall-clock ceiling for the whole review. Once it passes, queued calls are skipped and partial results post with a notice. A cancelled or timed-out job does the same (on SIGINT/SIGTERM). `0` disables |
| `max_review_tokens` | `0` (off) | Soft ceiling on billable tokens (input plus output) across every model call. Once it passes, no further calls start and the review posts what it has with a notice. Run once with `profile: true`, read the total, then set this above it |
| `max_concurrency` | `6` | Concurrent model calls across the whole review. Set `1` for a serial local run |
| `max_input_tokens` | `100000` | Token budget per model call before the diff is split into batches. Left unset, it is lowered to fit the model's context window when that is known |
| `max_tokens` | 16384 on ollama, openai-compatible and openrouter; the model's own ceiling elsewhere | Cap on the tokens each call may generate. `0` sends no cap. OpenRouter reserves prompt plus `max_tokens` against a prepaid balance, so the finite default keeps that bounded; raise it when a long answer is being cut off |
| `max_findings_per_lens` | `50` | Ceiling on findings from one (batch, lens) call, a backstop against a degenerate reply. When it fires, the highest-severity findings are kept and the review names the lens and the count dropped. `0` disables |
| `reasoning_effort` | route default | Bound how much a reasoning model thinks per call: `none`, `minimal`, `low`, `medium`, `high`, `xhigh`, or `default`. Use it when lens calls truncate or run long |
| `temperature` | `0.0` | Sampling temperature (`0.0` is deterministic) |
| `num_ctx` | `32768` | ollama context window (ignored for hosted providers) |
| `structured_output` | `true` | Constrain output to the findings JSON schema via `response_format` (JSON mode). Set `false` for an `openai-compatible` gateway that rejects it |
| `repair_unparseable` | `true` | When a reply cannot be parsed, send it back once (with the schema, without the diff) to be reformatted. Costs nothing on a healthy run |
| `retry_without_schema` | `true` | If the reformat also fails, re-run that lens once without `response_format`. Only applies to calls that sent the schema |

### Cloud Auth

| Input | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `aws_role_arn` | none | IAM role ARN to assume via OIDC for bedrock (keyless) |
| `aws_region` | `us-east-1` | AWS region for bedrock |
| `gcp_wif_provider` | none | Workload Identity Federation provider resource name for vertex |
| `gcp_service_account` | none | GCP service account email to impersonate via WIF |
| `azure_client_id` | none | Entra (Azure AD) client ID with a federated credential, for keyless azure via OIDC |
| `azure_tenant_id` | none | Entra (Azure AD) tenant ID for keyless azure |

### GitHub Identity and Runtime

| Input | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `config_path` | `.lgtmaybe.yml` | Path to the config file, relative to the repo root. With the default, a missing file is fine; a path you set must exist |
| `github_token` | `${{ github.token }}` | Token for reading the PR and posting the review |
| `github_identity` | `actions` | Comment author: `actions` posts as `github-actions[bot]`; `lgtmaybe` posts as `lgtmaybe[bot]` once the public App is installed and `id-token: write` is granted |
| `identity_broker_url` | managed endpoint | Advanced override for the public App identity exchange |
| `app_id` | none | Advanced: ID of your own GitHub App, used with `app_private_key`. Do not combine with `github_identity: lgtmaybe` |
| `app_private_key` | none | Advanced: private key of your own App named by `app_id` |
| `app_owner` | current repo's owner | Owner for a cross-repo App token |
| `app_repositories` | current repo | Repositories the App token may access, newline- or comma-separated. Use with `app_owner` |
| `image` | `ghcr.io/mattjcoles/lgtmaybe:v2` | Override the container image (advanced) |

The action passes `GITHUB_TOKEN` and the provider credentials into the
container itself, so you do not set them as `env`.

## Gate Merges on Findings

Set `fail_on` to a severity to turn the review into a merge gate. After posting
the review, lgtmaybe creates a **Check Run** named `lgtmaybe`. Its conclusion is
`failure` when any surviving finding is at or above that severity, and
`success` otherwise. lgtmaybe never sets PR approval state, so a clean review
stays comment-only.

```yaml
permissions:
  contents: read
  pull-requests: write
  checks: write # needed to create the Check Run

# ...

- uses: MattJColes/lgtmaybe@v2
  with:
    provider: openai
    model: gpt-5.5
    api_key: ${{ secrets.OPENAI_API_KEY }}
    fail_on: high # block merge on any high/critical finding
```

To make it block merges, mark the check as required in **branch protection**:

1. Open **Settings → Branches → Branch protection rules** (or a ruleset) for the
   target branch.
2. Enable **Require status checks to pass before merging**.
3. Search for and add the **`lgtmaybe`** check. It appears in the list once the
   Action has run with `fail_on` set on a PR against that branch.

A PR with a finding at or above the threshold then shows a failing `lgtmaybe`
check and cannot merge until the finding is resolved or `fail_on` is set to a higher
severity (for example `high` to `critical`).
Leave `fail_on` unset (the default) to keep reviews advisory; no check run is
created.

Creating the Check Run requires `checks: write`, as in the snippet above. The
public `lgtmaybe[bot]` App intentionally does not hold that permission, so
`github_identity: lgtmaybe` cannot be combined with `fail_on`. Use the default
Actions identity or a self-managed App granted `Checks: write`.

### What the Public App Cannot Do

The public `lgtmaybe[bot]` App holds a deliberately minimal permission set, so
two features are unavailable under `github_identity: lgtmaybe`:

| Feature | Behaviour under the public App |
|---|---|
| `fail_on` (merge-gate Check Run) | Refused up front with a setup error, because it needs `checks: write` |
| `resolve_fixed` (auto-resolve fixed conversations) | GitHub refuses `resolveReviewThread`, so threads stay open. The review is unaffected: nothing is posted to the thread, the refusal is logged once with what to do, and the run continues |

Both work under the default `actions` identity (with `pull-requests: write` in
the workflow `permissions:` block) or a self-managed App holding the matching
permission. Set `resolve_fixed: false` to stop attempting it.

## Adding a Config File

Place a `.lgtmaybe.yml` at the repo root to control severity thresholds, path
filters, file caps, and more. Set `config_path` if it lives elsewhere. See
[Configure .lgtmaybe.yml](./configure-lgtmaybe-yml.md) for all options.

## Pin to a Specific Version

`@v2` is a floating tag that tracks the latest `v2.x.x` release. To pin the
action exactly, use a full version tag:

```yaml
uses: MattJColes/lgtmaybe@v2.11.1
```

The action's default `image` is the floating `ghcr.io/mattjcoles/lgtmaybe:v2`,
so pinning the tag alone still runs the newest v2 container. To pin the
reviewer too, set the image to the matching version tag (no `v` prefix):

```yaml
uses: MattJColes/lgtmaybe@v2.11.1
with:
  image: ghcr.io/mattjcoles/lgtmaybe:2.11.1
  # ...provider, model, api_key as usual
```

## On Another Code Host

The review is identical on GitLab and Gitea; only the wiring and a few
host-capability differences change:

- [Review on GitLab](./review-on-gitlab.md): a CI job running
  `lgtmaybe gitlab-ci` on merge request pipelines.
- [Review on Gitea](./review-on-gitea.md): Gitea Actions, running the same
  container as GitHub.

Keyless cloud auth (Bedrock, Vertex, Azure) relies on GitHub Actions' OIDC
token, so it is available only on GitHub. On the other hosts use an API-key
provider or `ollama`.

---

<!-- Source: https://lgtmaybe.coles.codes/how-to/post-as-a-github-app/ -->

# Post as lgtmaybe[bot]

lgtmaybe is a GitHub Action. The Action runs the reviewer, and the provider,
model, and provider credentials stay in the workflow's `with:` block. A GitHub
App is optional: it only changes the author of lgtmaybe's GitHub comments from
`github-actions[bot]` to a branded bot.

You have three choices:

- **Do nothing:** the Action uses GitHub's workflow token and posts as
  `github-actions[bot]`.
- **Install the public lgtmaybe App:** the Action posts as `lgtmaybe[bot]`. You
  never receive or manage an App private key.
- **Use your own GitHub App:** an advanced, self-managed setup where you supply
  its App ID and private key.

## Install the public lgtmaybe App

1. [Install the lgtmaybe App](https://github.com/apps/lgtmaybe/installations/new)
   and select only the repositories where it should review pull requests.
2. Add `id-token: write` to the workflow permissions.
3. Set `github_identity: lgtmaybe` on the Action step.

Here is a complete OpenAI workflow. It gates reviews on trusted authors and
slash commands, as explained in
[Who can trigger a review](use-as-github-action.md#who-can-trigger-a-review):

```yaml
name: lgtmaybe

on:
  pull_request_target:
  issue_comment:
    types: [created]

permissions:
  contents: read
  id-token: write

jobs:
  review:
    if: >-
      (github.event_name == 'pull_request_target' &&
       contains(fromJson('["OWNER", "MEMBER", "COLLABORATOR"]'), github.event.pull_request.author_association)) ||
      (github.event.issue.pull_request &&
       contains(fromJson('["OWNER", "MEMBER", "COLLABORATOR"]'), github.event.comment.author_association) &&
       (contains(github.event.comment.body, '/review') ||
        contains(github.event.comment.body, '/improve') ||
        contains(github.event.comment.body, '/ask') ||
        contains(github.event.comment.body, '/describe') ||
        contains(github.event.comment.body, '/diagram')))
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7 # base repository only
      - uses: MattJColes/lgtmaybe@v2
        with:
          github_identity: lgtmaybe
          provider: openai
          model: gpt-5.5
          api_key: ${{ secrets.OPENAI_API_KEY }}
```

The provider configuration is unchanged: `github_identity` chooses who posts
on GitHub, not which model runs or where.

The public App has only:

- `contents: read`, to fetch repository and pull-request content
- `pull requests: write`, to post reviews, comments, and labels
- `issues: write`, to answer pull-request issue comments

The Action exchanges GitHub's signed workflow identity token for a short-lived
App token limited to the triggering repository and exactly those permissions.
The identity broker checks the repository, the event, and that the workflow
runs from the default branch. It never receives your diff, provider key,
prompt, model response, or review findings.

`github_identity: lgtmaybe` is an explicit choice. If `id-token: write` is
missing, the App is not installed on the repository, the workflow is not
trusted, or the identity service is unavailable, the job fails with setup
guidance. A misconfiguration is never papered over by quietly posting as
`github-actions[bot]`.

Reviews and the `/review`, `/improve`, `/ask`, `/describe`, and `/diagram`
commands arrive on `pull_request_target` or `issue_comment`, which run from the
default branch, so they post as `lgtmaybe[bot]`. Replies inside review threads
do not start a model run; the next review checks a pushed fix.

To remove access, uninstall the App or remove the repository from the
installation. To return to `github-actions[bot]`, remove
`github_identity: lgtmaybe` and `id-token: write` from the workflow (and add
back `pull-requests: write`). The Action revokes its temporary App token after
each run, and GitHub expires it anyway if that cleanup cannot run.

The public App intentionally has no `Checks: write` permission, so
`github_identity: lgtmaybe` cannot be combined with `fail_on`. When lgtmaybe
must create a merge gate, keep the default `github_identity: actions` and grant
the workflow `checks: write`, or use a self-managed App with `Checks: write`.
The public App also cannot resolve fixed conversations: GitHub refuses
`resolveReviewThread` for it, so those threads stay open. See
[What the public App cannot do](use-as-github-action.md#what-the-public-app-cannot-do).

## Use your own GitHub App

Use this path only when your organisation already runs a GitHub App and wants
reviews attributed to it.

Give the App the repository permissions `contents: read`,
`pull requests: write`, and `issues: write`, plus `checks: write` if you use
`fail_on`. Install it on the repositories it may review. Store its ID as the
`LGTMAYBE_APP_ID` repository variable and its PEM private key as the
`LGTMAYBE_APP_PRIVATE_KEY` Actions secret:

```yaml
permissions:
  contents: read

steps:
  - uses: actions/checkout@v7
  - uses: MattJColes/lgtmaybe@v2
    with:
      provider: openai
      model: gpt-5.5
      api_key: ${{ secrets.OPENAI_API_KEY }}
      app_id: ${{ vars.LGTMAYBE_APP_ID }}
      app_private_key: ${{ secrets.LGTMAYBE_APP_PRIVATE_KEY }}
```

The Action mints a short-lived token for the current repository from these and
revokes it at the end of the job. To review across repositories, set
`app_owner` and `app_repositories` (see the
[Action inputs](use-as-github-action.md#github-identity-and-runtime)).

Do not combine `app_id` / `app_private_key` with
`github_identity: lgtmaybe`. The Action checks this before minting a token.

---

<!-- Source: https://lgtmaybe.coles.codes/how-to/review-on-azure-devops/ -->

# Review Pull Requests on Azure DevOps

lgtmaybe posts reviews to Azure DevOps Repos as well as GitHub, GitLab and
Gitea. The review itself is identical (same lenses, same reflection pass, same
findings) because none of it depends on the host. Only the adapter that reads
the change and posts the comments differs.

Azure DevOps Services is supported: `dev.azure.com/{organisation}` and the
legacy `{organisation}.visualstudio.com`. Azure DevOps Server (on-premises) is
not supported yet.

## Set It Up

Azure Pipelines runs a pull request build from the YAML in the pull request
itself, so the job that holds the model key must not live in the repository
being reviewed. The setup below keeps it in a template in a separate, protected
repository, and the reviewed repository only extends it. Read
[Security: who can change the pipeline](#security-who-can-change-the-pipeline)
before choosing anything simpler.

1. **Create a protected template repository.** For example
   `Platform/pipeline-templates`. Add branch policies to its `main` branch so
   nobody can change it without a review from someone trusted with the secrets.
   Commit
   [`examples/azure-devops/lgtmaybe-review.yml`](https://github.com/MattJColes/lgtmaybe/blob/main/examples/azure-devops/lgtmaybe-review.yml)
   to it.

2. **Store the model key in a variable group.** In *Pipelines → Library*,
   create a variable group named `lgtmaybe-secrets` holding the provider key as
   a secret, for example `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`. Use a key with a spend limit.

3. **Require the template.** On that variable group, open *Approvals and
   checks*, add a **Required template** check, and name the template
   repository, `refs/heads/main` and `lgtmaybe-review.yml`. A pipeline that does
   not extend exactly that template is refused the key, whatever its YAML says.

4. **Let the pipeline comment.** lgtmaybe posts with the job's own token,
   `System.AccessToken`. In *Project settings → Repositories → Security*,
   select the project's build service identity
   (`<Project> Build Service (<Organisation>)`) on the reviewed repository and
   allow **Contribute to pull requests**, and nothing broader.

5. **Add the pipeline to the reviewed repository.** Copy
   [`examples/azure-devops/azure-pipelines.yml`](https://github.com/MattJColes/lgtmaybe/blob/main/examples/azure-devops/azure-pipelines.yml),
   point its `resources.repositories` entry at your template repository, and
   create a pipeline from it. Approve its access to the template repository and
   the variable group on the first run.

6. **Run it on pull requests.** Azure Repos starts pull request builds from a
   branch policy, not from a `pr:` trigger. In *Project settings →
   Repositories → Policies*, open the target branch and add the pipeline under
   **Build validation**.

The reviewed repository's pipeline holds no steps and no secrets:

```yaml
trigger: none

resources:
  repositories:
    - repository: trusted
      type: git
      name: Platform/pipeline-templates
      ref: refs/heads/main

extends:
  template: lgtmaybe-review.yml@trusted
```

The template in the protected repository runs the GHCR image with the
`azure-pipelines` command:

```yaml
jobs:
  - job: lgtmaybe
    pool:
      vmImage: ubuntu-latest
    variables:
      - group: lgtmaybe-secrets
    steps:
      - checkout: none

      - script: |
          docker run --rm \
            -e SYSTEM_COLLECTIONURI -e SYSTEM_TEAMPROJECT \
            -e BUILD_REPOSITORY_NAME -e BUILD_REPOSITORY_PROVIDER \
            -e SYSTEM_PULLREQUEST_PULLREQUESTID \
            -e SYSTEM_ACCESSTOKEN -e ANTHROPIC_API_KEY \
            ghcr.io/mattjcoles/lgtmaybe:v2 \
            azure-pipelines --provider anthropic --model claude-sonnet-4-6
        displayName: lgtmaybe review
        env:
          SYSTEM_ACCESSTOKEN: $(System.AccessToken)
          ANTHROPIC_API_KEY: $(ANTHROPIC_API_KEY)
```

Secret variables, `System.AccessToken` included, reach a script only when they
are mapped under `env:`, which is why both are listed there. The template takes
no parameters on purpose: a parameter would let the pull request's YAML pass
steps into the job that holds the secrets.

`azure-pipelines` finds the pull request from the predefined variables
`SYSTEM_COLLECTIONURI`, `SYSTEM_TEAMPROJECT`, `BUILD_REPOSITORY_NAME` and
`SYSTEM_PULLREQUEST_PULLREQUESTID`. On a build that is not validating a pull
request there is no id, and lgtmaybe fails with an error naming the missing
variable rather than guessing. A pipeline building a GitHub repository is
refused too: those pull requests live on GitHub, so use the
[GitHub Action](use-as-github-action.md). Azure Pipelines always sets
`BUILD_REPOSITORY_PROVIDER`; when it is unset (running the command by hand),
the repository is treated as Azure Repos.

Configure the review with the command's flags: `--provider`, `--model`,
`--fallback-model`, `--api-key`, `--api-base` and `--config`.

### Without Docker

On a self-hosted agent without Docker, install the CLI instead. These steps
replace the `steps:` of the protected template, never the reviewed
repository's pipeline:

```yaml
    steps:
      - checkout: none
      - task: UsePythonVersion@0
        inputs:
          versionSpec: "3.12"
      - script: |
          pip install lgtmaybe
          lgtmaybe azure-pipelines --provider anthropic --model claude-sonnet-4-6
        displayName: lgtmaybe review
        env:
          SYSTEM_ACCESSTOKEN: $(System.AccessToken)
          ANTHROPIC_API_KEY: $(ANTHROPIC_API_KEY)
```

## Tokens

lgtmaybe reads the Azure DevOps token from one of two variables:

| Variable | What it is | Sent as |
|---|---|---|
| `AZURE_DEVOPS_TOKEN` | A personal access token with **Code (Read & write)** scope | Basic auth, empty user name |
| `SYSTEM_ACCESSTOKEN` | The job's own token, mapped from `$(System.AccessToken)` | Bearer token |

When both are set, `AZURE_DEVOPS_TOKEN` wins. Use a personal access token when
the comments should come from a named account rather than the build service.
Either way the token travels only in the `Authorization` header and is never
logged.

## Try It Locally First

Reviewing a pull request by URL happens in the pipeline, where the token and
the pull request live. Locally, `lgtmaybe review` reviews the branch you have
checked out against the remote primary branch, and prints the findings instead
of posting them:

```bash
git switch my-feature-branch
export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=...
lgtmaybe review --provider anthropic --model claude-sonnet-4-6
```

## How It Differs from GitHub

Azure DevOps serves no unified diff. lgtmaybe reads the pull request's latest
iteration, lists the files it changes against the merge base, fetches each
file's text before and after, and builds the diff itself. Lockfiles, vendored
and binary files are listed as changed but never fetched, and a file side over
1 MB is treated like a binary. A pull request changing more than 300 files is
not reviewed; lgtmaybe says so instead of reviewing part of it. The same goes
when Azure DevOps reports no merge base for the pull request. A file Azure
DevOps keeps throttling or failing to return is retried, then left out on its
own and named under **Files not reviewed** in the summary; a 401 or 403 fails
the review, since that means the token is wrong.

Each finding is its own comment thread on the changed line, left **active** so
a "resolve all comments" branch policy can hold the merge until someone deals
with it. The summary is a general thread that is edited in place on each run.
It is created **closed**, so it never holds a merge on its own. A finding whose
thread is already open, or marked *Won't fix* or *Closed*, is not posted again;
a finding whose thread was marked *Resolved* and that comes back is.

On a later run, a finding thread lgtmaybe opened is marked *Resolved*, with a
`✅ Looks resolved.` reply, when the finding is no longer reported **and** the
line it was posted on has changed since. Azure DevOps has no "this code moved"
flag, so lgtmaybe records the iteration each thread was posted at and compares
the file then with the file now. Threads anyone else opened are never touched,
and nothing is resolved after a run that failed or finished only partly. The
token needs the same *Contribute to pull requests* permission it already uses
to post. Set `resolve_fixed: false` in `.lgtmaybe.yml` to resolve threads by
hand. A thread posted by an earlier lgtmaybe version may carry no iteration,
and one that doesn't stays open for a person to resolve.

These are not available yet:

| Not available | Why | What happens instead |
|---|---|---|
| Incremental review | Not built yet | Every run is a full review |
| Slash commands (`/review`, `/ask`, …) | `azure-pipelines` reviews the pull request; nothing routes comments to it | Queue the build again to review again |
| Change overview comment | `azure-pipelines` runs the review only | No description or diagram thread is posted |
| PR labels and the `fail_on` merge gate | Not built yet in the Azure DevOps adapter | No labels or pull request status are set |
| 👎 feedback (`learn_feedback`) | Not built yet | A downvoted finding can be posted again on a later run |
| Symbol resolution | No base-branch clone in the Azure DevOps adapter | Reflection judges cross-file findings without the symbol's definition |
| One-click suggestions | Azure DevOps has no suggestion blocks | A suggested fix shows as a code block |
| Azure DevOps Server | Only Azure DevOps Services URLs are recognised | The URL is refused with an error naming Azure DevOps Server |

Keyless model auth (Bedrock, Vertex, Azure OpenAI through GitHub OIDC) is built
into the GitHub composite action, not the `azure-pipelines` command. Use an API
key, or `ollama` against a model on the agent.

## Security: Who Can Change the Pipeline

A pull request build in Azure Pipelines runs the YAML from the pull request's
own merge result. This is the opposite of GitHub's `pull_request_target`, where
the base branch's workflow runs. Anyone who can push a branch and open a pull
request can therefore rewrite a pipeline file in that repository, keep its
variable mappings, and send every secret those steps can read to a server of
their choosing. `checkout: none` does not help: the YAML itself is the part the
pull request controls.

So a pipeline file in the reviewed repository that maps a secret is only safe
when everyone who can open a pull request there is already trusted with that
secret. Otherwise use the setup above:

- The secret-bearing job lives in a template in a separate repository with
  branch policies, and the reviewed repository only `extends` it.
- The model key sits in a variable group guarded by a **Required template**
  check, so a pipeline that drops the `extends`, or points it at another branch
  or file, is refused the key.
- **Builds of pull requests from forks get no secrets by default. Keep that
  setting off.**
- Grant the build service only **Contribute to pull requests** on the reviewed
  repository, and keep *Limit job authorization scope to current project*
  turned on. Any pipeline can map its own `System.AccessToken`, so its
  permissions are what a rewritten pipeline could use.
- Prefer `System.AccessToken` over a personal access token. If you must use a
  personal access token, give it only **Code (Read & write)** on this
  organisation, a short expiry, and keep it in the protected variable group.
- Use a model key with a spend limit, so a leaked key has a ceiling.

lgtmaybe itself never checks out or executes pull request code. It reads the
change through the API and treats every byte of it as untrusted input.

---

<!-- Source: https://lgtmaybe.coles.codes/how-to/review-on-gitea/ -->

# Review Pull Requests on Gitea

lgtmaybe posts reviews to Gitea as well as GitHub. The review itself is
identical (same lenses, same reflection pass, same findings) because none of it
depends on the host. Only the adapter that fetches the diff and posts the
comments differs.

## Set It Up

The example workflow needs Gitea 1.21 or later, for the `pull_request_target`
trigger. Read
[Security: Who Can Change the Workflow](#security-who-can-change-the-workflow)
for why it matters.

1. **Create a token.** Sign in as a dedicated account with write access to the
   reviewed repository only. In Gitea, go to *Settings → Applications → Access
   Tokens* and create a token with the `write:repository`, `write:issue` and
   `read:user` scopes (`read:user` lets lgtmaybe tell its own comments apart). Add it to your repository as a secret named `LGTMAYBE_GITEA_TOKEN`.
   Gitea refuses secret names that start with `GITEA_` or `GITHUB_`, and the
   example maps this secret to the `GITEA_TOKEN` variable lgtmaybe reads.

    You need all three. `write:repository` also covers reading, and Gitea files the
    review endpoint lgtmaybe posts inline comments through
    (`POST /pulls/{index}/reviews`) and the commit-status endpoint under the
    *repository* category, not *issue*, so a token with only `read:repository`
    is refused on the one call the setup exists to make. `write:issue` covers
    the summary comment and the PR labels. `read:user` lets lgtmaybe ask Gitea
    who the token is (`GET /user`): only comments that identity wrote count as
    lgtmaybe's, so nobody else can edit the summary through us or paste a hidden
    id that hides a finding. Without it every re-run posts a fresh summary and
    re-posts its findings rather than trusting comments it cannot attribute.

2. **Add a provider key.** Add the API key for whichever model you want as a
   second secret, for example `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`. Use a key with a spend
   limit.

3. **Add the workflow.** Copy
   [`examples/gitea/lgtmaybe.yml`](https://github.com/MattJColes/lgtmaybe/blob/main/examples/gitea/lgtmaybe.yml)
   into your repository at `.gitea/workflows/lgtmaybe.yml`.

That is the whole setup. Gitea Actions reimplements the GitHub Actions runtime,
so the example runs lgtmaybe's container image with the same `action` command
and `INPUT_*` variables. lgtmaybe reads `GITHUB_SERVER_URL`, which Gitea points
at your own instance, to know which host to post to.

## Try It Locally First

Reviewing a pull request by URL happens in the Actions run, where the token and
the PR context live. Locally, `lgtmaybe review` reviews the branch you have
checked out against the remote primary branch, and prints the findings instead
of posting them:

```bash
git switch my-feature-branch
export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=...
lgtmaybe review --provider anthropic --model claude-sonnet-4-6
```

It runs the same review, so it is a quick way to see what a model will say about
your change before you wire up the workflow.

## What Works, and What Does Not

The review itself works in full: every lens, the self-reflection pass, secret
redaction, prompt-injection hardening, static-analysis fusion, path filters,
finding rules, the change overview comment, PR labels (only labels that already
exist in the repository; lgtmaybe does not create them), the `fail_on` merge gate
(as a commit status), and the `/review`, `/improve`, `/ask`, `/describe` and
`/diagram` slash commands.

A slash command runs only for a commenter with write access to the repository.
Gitea's workflow `if:` cannot read the commenter's role the way GitHub's
`author_association` does, so lgtmaybe checks it itself through the collaborator
permission API. Anyone else's command is ignored with a log line, exits
successfully, and makes no model call.

These are unavailable on Gitea, and lgtmaybe skips them rather than failing:

| Not available | Why | What happens instead |
|---|---|---|
| Incremental review | Gitea's compare endpoint returns commit metadata, not a unified diff | Every run is a full review |
| Resolve-on-fix | Gitea has no thread-resolution API | Fixed findings' comments stay open |
| 👎 feedback (`learn_feedback`) | Not implemented in the Gitea adapter | A downvoted finding can be posted again on a later run |
| Symbol resolution | No base-branch clone in the Gitea adapter | Reflection judges cross-file findings without the symbol's definition |
| Keyless cloud auth | The OIDC/WIF exchange is built into the GitHub composite action | Use an API key, or `ollama` for a local model |

A submitted Gitea review cannot be edited, so lgtmaybe reads the hidden finding
IDs already on the pull request and does not post the same finding twice. The
summary lives in an ordinary comment, which is editable, so it updates in place
on each run.

## Security: Who Can Change the Workflow

A `pull_request` run in Gitea Actions takes its workflow file from the pull
request's own head commit. A pull request from a branch in the same repository
runs whatever workflow it contains, with the repository's secrets, so anyone who
can push a branch could rewrite the review job and send the model key and the
token to a server of their choosing. A pull request from a fork also runs its
own workflow, but Gitea passes it no repository or organisation secrets, only
the automatic job token, so lgtmaybe cannot review it.

`pull_request_target`, available from Gitea 1.21, takes the workflow from the
base branch instead, as on GitHub, and gives it the repository's secrets for
pull requests from forks too. That is why the example uses it, and why it is the
same trade-off as on GitHub: lgtmaybe never checks out or executes pull-request
code. It reads the diff through the API and treats every byte of it as
untrusted input. The `issue_comment` arm always runs the workflow from the
default branch, so a pull request cannot change that either. Gitea still treats
a comment on a fork's pull request as a fork run and passes it no secrets, so
slash commands work only on pull requests from branches in the repository.

What `pull_request_target` does not cover:

- **Anyone with write access can still read the secrets.** Repository and
  organisation secrets reach every workflow run in the repository, including a
  `push` workflow on a branch someone has just pushed, with no pull request
  involved. Give write access only to people trusted with the secrets, and take
  other contributions as pull requests from forks.
- **Gitea before 1.21 has no `pull_request_target`.** There, switch the example
  to `pull_request` only if everyone who can push a branch is trusted with the
  secrets. Pull requests from forks are not reviewed, because their runs get no
  secrets.
- **A fork's pull request starts a paid review without approval.** On an
  instance with open registration, anyone can open one. Use a model key with a
  spend limit.

Keep the token narrow too. A Gitea access token works on every repository its
owner can reach, which is why step 1 creates it on a dedicated account with
write access to the reviewed repository only, and gives it only the two scopes
lgtmaybe needs. Do not use `secrets.GITEA_TOKEN` in its place: that name always
resolves to the automatic job token, because Gitea refuses a secret of your own
with that name.

---

<!-- Source: https://lgtmaybe.coles.codes/how-to/review-on-gitlab/ -->

# Review Merge Requests on GitLab

lgtmaybe posts reviews to GitLab as well as GitHub. The review itself is
identical (same lenses, same reflection pass, same findings) because none of it
depends on the host. Only the adapter that fetches the diff and posts the
comments differs.

## Set It Up

A merge request pipeline runs the CI configuration from the merge request's own
source branch, so where the job lives decides who can read its secrets. Read
[Security: Who Can Change the Pipeline](#security-who-can-change-the-pipeline)
before choosing where it goes.

1. **Create a token.** In your project, go to *Settings → Access Tokens* and
   create a project access token with the `api` scope, the Developer role and an
   expiry date. Add it under *Settings → CI/CD → Variables* as `GITLAB_TOKEN`,
   masked, with **Environment scope** set to `lgtmaybe`.

2. **Add a provider key.** Add the API key for whichever model you want as a
   second masked variable scoped to the `lgtmaybe` environment, for example
   `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`. Use a key with a spend limit.

3. **Add the job.** Copy
   [`examples/gitlab/.gitlab-ci.yml`](https://github.com/MattJColes/lgtmaybe/blob/main/examples/gitlab/.gitlab-ci.yml)
   into your repository, or merge its `lgtmaybe` job into your existing
   pipeline. If not everyone who can push a branch is trusted with the secrets,
   put it in a separate configuration project instead, as described under
   [Keep the Pipeline Configuration Outside the Project](#keep-the-pipeline-configuration-outside-the-project).

The job names the environment `lgtmaybe` with `action: access`. That is what
lets it read the variables scoped to that environment, without recording a
deployment, while the pipeline's other jobs never receive them.

The job runs `python -m lgtmaybe gitlab-ci`, which finds the merge request from
GitLab's predefined variables (`CI_SERVER_URL` or `CI_SERVER_HOST`,
`CI_MERGE_REQUEST_PROJECT_PATH` or `CI_PROJECT_PATH`, and
`CI_MERGE_REQUEST_IID`). It must therefore run on merge request pipelines:

```yaml
rules:
  - if: $CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE == "merge_request_event"
```

On a branch pipeline there is no merge request to review, and lgtmaybe fails
with an error naming the missing `CI_MERGE_REQUEST_IID` rather than guessing.

The example job does not clone the repository (`GIT_STRATEGY: none`), so there
is no `.lgtmaybe.yml` to read. Configure the review with the command's flags:
`--provider`, `--model`, `--fallback-model`, `--api-key`, `--api-base`,
`--config` and `--no-incremental`.

## Try It Locally First

Reviewing a merge request by URL happens in CI, where the token and the MR
context live. Locally, `lgtmaybe review` reviews the branch you have checked out
against the remote primary branch, and prints the findings instead of posting
them:

```bash
git switch my-feature-branch
export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=...
lgtmaybe review --provider anthropic --model claude-sonnet-4-6
```

It runs the same review, so it is a quick way to see what a model will say about
your change before you wire up the pipeline.

## How It Differs from GitHub

GitLab has no batched review object, so each finding is posted as its own
discussion, anchored by the merge request's diff refs and the old or new file
line. The summary is a note that updates in place on each run.

Resolve-on-fix works here: GitLab discussions resolve over plain REST, where
GitHub needs GraphQL. A finding's discussion is resolved only once the follow-up
validation pass on an incremental run has confirmed it is fixed, never merely
because the finding stopped being reported. GitHub also requires the thread to
be marked outdated (the code under it changed). GitLab's API has no such flag,
so lgtmaybe works it out: a discussion counts as outdated when the diff since
the commit it was posted on touches the hunk around its line.

The GitLab adapter also supports PR labels and the `fail_on` merge gate
(reported as a commit status). Both are config-file settings, so they need a job
that provides a file for `--config`.

### Incremental Re-review

The first pipeline on a merge request reviews the whole change. Every later
pipeline reviews only the commits pushed since the last completed review, read
from a hidden watermark in lgtmaybe's summary note. lgtmaybe trusts that
watermark only in a note written by its own token's user, so another user's
note cannot skip a review.

It falls back to a full review whenever the increment can't be trusted:

- the branch was rebased or force-pushed (the new commits don't build on the
  last reviewed one);
- the new commits include a merge;
- GitLab no longer knows the last reviewed commit, timed out, or left part of
  the diff out because it is too large;
- any API call fails.

A failed or partial run leaves the watermark where it was, so the next run
still covers the commits it missed. Running a pipeline again on a head that was
already reviewed completely posts nothing.

GitLab has no `/review full`. To force a full re-review, run the pipeline with
the CI/CD variable `LGTMAYBE_INCREMENTAL` set to `false`, pass
`--no-incremental`, or set `incremental: false` in the config file.

### 👎 Feedback

Award a 👎 (`thumbsdown`) emoji to the first note of one of lgtmaybe's finding
discussions and later runs stop raising that finding on the merge request. Only
a 👎 from a member with the Developer role or above counts, because anyone can
award an emoji on a public project. A high or critical security finding is
never hidden this way. Set `learn_feedback: false` to turn it off.

These are not available:

| Not available | Why | What happens instead |
|---|---|---|
| Slash commands (`/review`, `/ask`, …) | `gitlab-ci` reviews the merge request; nothing routes MR comments to it | Re-run the pipeline to review again |
| Change overview comment | `gitlab-ci` runs the review only | No description or diagram comment is posted |
| Symbol resolution | No base-branch clone in the GitLab adapter | Reflection judges cross-file findings without the symbol's definition |
| Keyless cloud auth | The OIDC/WIF exchange is built into the GitHub composite action | Use an API key, or `ollama` |

## Security: Who Can Change the Pipeline

A merge request pipeline runs the `.gitlab-ci.yml` from the merge request's
source branch, not from the target branch. This is the opposite of GitHub's
`pull_request_target`, where the base branch's workflow runs, and GitLab has no
equivalent. Anyone who can push a branch to the project (the Developer role and
above) can therefore edit the `lgtmaybe` job, keep its variables, and send the
model key and `GITLAB_TOKEN` to a server of their choosing. A branch pipeline
gives them the same access without opening a merge request at all.
`GIT_STRATEGY: none` does not help: the YAML itself is the part they control.

So a job in the reviewed project's own CI configuration is only safe when
everyone who can push a branch there is already trusted with both secrets. For a
team where that holds, the setup above is enough. Otherwise, choose one of the
setups below. Each has a cost, and none of them is as simple as
`pull_request_target`.

Scoping the variables to the `lgtmaybe` environment is worth doing either way,
but it is not a defence against this. It keeps the secrets away from jobs that
never ask for them, such as a compromised test tool, and a job the merge request
controls can still name the environment.

### Merge Requests from Forks

A merge request from a fork is safe by default. Its pipeline runs in the fork,
with the fork's CI configuration and the fork's variables, and never receives
the parent project's variables. Keep it that way:

- Do not use **Run pipeline** on a fork's merge request in the parent project.
  That runs the fork's CI configuration in the parent project with all of the
  parent's variables, which hands the fork's author your secrets. GitLab shows a
  warning before it does this.
- To remove the option, disable `ci_allow_fork_pipelines_to_run_in_parent_project`
  with the [projects API](https://docs.gitlab.com/api/projects/#update-a-project).

The cost is that lgtmaybe does not review fork merge requests: their pipelines
have no key.

### Protected Variables

Marking `GITLAB_TOKEN` and the model key **Protected** keeps them out of every
pipeline on an unprotected branch, so pushing a branch no longer reveals them.
A merge request pipeline receives protected variables only when all of these
hold (the setting below arrived in GitLab 18.1):

- the project allows it, under *Settings → CI/CD → Variables → Access protected
  resources in merge request pipelines*;
- both the source and target branches are protected, and in the same project;
- the user who starts the pipeline can push or merge to the target branch.

A merge request pipeline from a fork never receives them.

The cost: lgtmaybe then reviews only merge requests between protected branches,
opened by people who could already change the pipeline there. A merge request
from an ordinary feature branch gets no token and the job fails. To skip the job
there instead, extend its rule:

```yaml
rules:
  - if: $CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE == "merge_request_event" && $CI_MERGE_REQUEST_SOURCE_BRANCH_PROTECTED == "true"
```

### Keep the Pipeline Configuration Outside the Project

This works on every GitLab tier. In the reviewed project, set *Settings → CI/CD →
General pipelines → CI/CD configuration file* to a file in a separate project,
for example `.gitlab-ci.yml@my-group/ci-config` (append `:branch-name` to pin a
branch). Every pipeline in the reviewed project, merge request and branch
pipelines alike, then runs that file, so no commit to the reviewed project can
change a job. Changing the setting needs the Maintainer role. Protect the
configuration project's default branch and give write access only to people
trusted with the secrets.

The variables stay unprotected, so merge requests from feature branches are
reviewed. What it costs:

- That file is now the project's whole pipeline, so the project's build and test
  jobs must live there too. Do not `include` the reviewed project's own CI files
  from it: a file read at the merge request's commit is the merge request's to
  edit, and its jobs could name the `lgtmaybe` environment.
- Those build and test jobs still run the merge request's code. Keep both
  variables scoped to the `lgtmaybe` environment so those jobs never receive
  them, and keep that environment out of every job but the review.
- Do not let a job that runs merge request code share a shell-executor runner
  with the review job. There, jobs run as the same user on the same host, and
  one can read another's environment.
- Keep *Settings → CI/CD → Variables → Minimum role to use pipeline variables*
  at Maintainer or above (the self-managed default), or `no_one_allowed` (the
  default for new projects on GitLab.com). A pipeline variable outranks a
  project variable, so anyone who can set one can change the review job's
  environment. `AZURE_API_BASE`, for example, tells lgtmaybe where to send the
  key when the job passes no `--api-base`.

### Pipeline Execution Policies

A [pipeline execution policy](https://docs.gitlab.com/user/application_security/policies/pipeline_execution_policies/)
(GitLab Ultimate) can add the `lgtmaybe` job to every pipeline from a separate
security policy project, so a merge request cannot change that job. On its own
it does not keep the secrets safe. Unless the policy replaces the project's
configuration entirely (`override_project_ci`), the project's own
`.gitlab-ci.yml` still runs from the merge request's branch, and its jobs
receive the same project and group variables, or can name the `lgtmaybe`
environment to get them. A policy that does replace the configuration has the
same costs as the previous section.

### Tokens and Keys

Whichever setup you choose, assume a secret can leak and limit what it is worth:

- Make `GITLAB_TOKEN` a project access token on this project only, with the
  `api` scope (posting discussions needs it; `read_api` cannot), the Developer
  role and nothing higher, and a short expiry. On GitLab.com, project access
  tokens need Premium or Ultimate. On the Free tier, use a personal access token
  of a dedicated account that is a Developer of this project alone. A leaked
  token can post as lgtmaybe, including a summary note whose watermark makes
  the next incremental run skip the commits before it.
- Use a model key with a spend limit, so a leaked key has a ceiling.

lgtmaybe itself never checks out or executes merge request code. It reads the
diff through the API and treats every byte of it as untrusted input, which is
why the example job sets `GIT_STRATEGY: none` and does not clone the repository
at all.

---

<!-- Source: https://lgtmaybe.coles.codes/how-to/review-with-openai/ -->

# Review with OpenAI

OpenAI is a key-based provider: add an `OPENAI_API_KEY` and pick a model. There
is no OIDC and no endpoint to configure, which makes it the simplest path to a
hosted review.

## Contents

- [Get an API key](#get-an-api-key)
- [GitHub Action](#github-action)
- [Run locally](#run-locally)
- [Choosing the model](#choosing-the-model)
- [Persist non-secret defaults](#persist-non-secret-defaults)

## Get an API Key

Create a key at <https://platform.openai.com/api-keys>. In your repository, add
it as an Actions secret named `OPENAI_API_KEY`
(**Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions → New repository secret**).

## GitHub Action

Copy [`examples/workflows/review-openai.yml`][wf] to
`.github/workflows/lgtmaybe.yml`. The core step is:

```yaml
- uses: MattJColes/lgtmaybe@v2
  with:
    provider: openai
    model: gpt-5.5
    api_key: ${{ secrets.OPENAI_API_KEY }}
```

The workflow runs on `pull_request_target`, so the secret is available, but PR
code is never checked out: lgtmaybe reads the diff through the API. See
[Use as a GitHub Action](use-as-github-action.md) for the full workflow,
including [who can trigger a review](use-as-github-action.md#who-can-trigger-a-review).

## Run Locally

```bash
export OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-...

lgtmaybe review --provider openai --model gpt-5.5
```

You can pass the key with `--api-key sk-...` instead of the env var. Either way,
the key is never persisted to config.

## Choosing the Model

Use any chat model your key can access, named as you would send it to the
OpenAI API (litellm's native form): `gpt-5.5` or one of the newer GPT-6 models
(`gpt-6-sol`, `gpt-6-luna`, `gpt-6-astra`), or a smaller model to cut cost.
[Choose a review model](choose-a-review-model.md) has measured results for the
GPT-6 family.

Under the default `fast` preset, a `gpt-5*` review model has its reflection
(false-positive audit) pass run on `gpt-5-mini`, so your key needs access to
that model too. Set `reflect_model` to choose a different auditor.

## Persist Non-Secret Defaults

Provider and model are not secrets, so they can live in `.lgtmaybe.yml`. The key
stays in the environment.

```yaml
provider: openai
model: gpt-5.5
```

With that file in place, `lgtmaybe review` needs no flags. See
[Configure .lgtmaybe.yml](configure-lgtmaybe-yml.md) for every setting.

[wf]: https://github.com/MattJColes/lgtmaybe/blob/main/examples/workflows/review-openai.yml

---

# Review with Claude (Anthropic)

Anthropic is a key-based provider: add an `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` and pick a Claude
model. There is no OIDC and no endpoint to configure.

## Contents

- [Get an API key](#get-an-api-key)
- [GitHub Action](#github-action)
- [Run locally](#run-locally)
- [Choosing the model](#choosing-the-model)
- [Want it through a gateway instead?](#want-it-through-a-gateway-instead)
- [Persist non-secret defaults](#persist-non-secret-defaults)

## Get an API Key

Create a key in the [Anthropic Console](https://console.anthropic.com/). In your
repository, add it as an Actions secret named `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`
(**Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions → New repository secret**).

## GitHub Action

Copy [`examples/workflows/review-anthropic.yml`][wf] to
`.github/workflows/lgtmaybe.yml`. The core step is:

```yaml
- uses: MattJColes/lgtmaybe@v2
  with:
    provider: anthropic
    model: claude-sonnet-4-6
    api_key: ${{ secrets.ANTHROPIC_API_KEY }}
```

The workflow runs on `pull_request_target`, so the secret is available, but PR
code is never checked out: lgtmaybe reads the diff through the API. See
[Use as a GitHub Action](use-as-github-action.md) for the full workflow,
including [who can trigger a review](use-as-github-action.md#who-can-trigger-a-review).

## Run Locally

```bash
export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-ant-...

lgtmaybe review --provider anthropic --model claude-sonnet-4-6
```

You can pass the key with `--api-key sk-ant-...` instead of the env var. Either
way, the key is never persisted to config.

## Choosing the Model

Pass litellm's native Anthropic name as the model. `claude-sonnet-4-6` is a
strong default. Use an Opus-class model (such as `claude-opus-5-5`) for the
deepest review at a higher price, or a Haiku-class model (such as
`claude-haiku-4-5`) to cut cost on smaller PRs.

Under the default `fast` preset, a Sonnet or Opus review model has its
reflection (false-positive audit) pass run on `claude-haiku-4-5`, so your key
needs access to that model too. Set `reflect_model` to choose a different
auditor.

## Want It Through a Gateway Instead?

If you reach Claude through OpenRouter, Bedrock or Vertex rather than the
Anthropic API, use that provider instead:

- [OpenRouter](review-with-openrouter.md): `anthropic/claude-sonnet-4.6`
- [Bedrock (keyless OIDC)](review-with-bedrock-oidc.md)
- [Vertex (keyless WIF)](review-with-vertex-wif.md)

## Persist Non-Secret Defaults

Provider and model are not secrets, so they can live in `.lgtmaybe.yml`. The key
stays in the environment.

```yaml
provider: anthropic
model: claude-sonnet-4-6
```

With that file in place, `lgtmaybe review` needs no flags. See
[Configure .lgtmaybe.yml](configure-lgtmaybe-yml.md) for every setting.

[wf]: https://github.com/MattJColes/lgtmaybe/blob/main/examples/workflows/review-anthropic.yml

# Review with OpenRouter

[OpenRouter](https://openrouter.ai/) is a key-based gateway to many model
vendors behind one API. Add an `OPENROUTER_API_KEY`, then pick any model
OpenRouter offers by its `vendor/model` name.

## Contents

- [Get an API key](#get-an-api-key)
- [GitHub Action](#github-action)
- [Run locally](#run-locally)
- [Choosing the model](#choosing-the-model)
- [Credit reservations](#credit-reservations)
- [Rate limits](#rate-limits)
- [Persist non-secret defaults](#persist-non-secret-defaults)

## Get an API Key

Create a key at <https://openrouter.ai/keys>. In your repository, add it as an
Actions secret named `OPENROUTER_API_KEY`
(**Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions → New repository secret**).

## GitHub Action

Copy [`examples/workflows/review-openrouter.yml`][wf] to
`.github/workflows/lgtmaybe.yml`. The core step is:

```yaml
- uses: MattJColes/lgtmaybe@v2
  with:
    provider: openrouter
    model: anthropic/claude-sonnet-4.6
    api_key: ${{ secrets.OPENROUTER_API_KEY }}
```

The workflow runs on `pull_request_target`, so the secret is available, but PR
code is never checked out: lgtmaybe reads the diff through the API. See
[Use as a GitHub Action](use-as-github-action.md) for the full workflow,
including [who can trigger a review](use-as-github-action.md#who-can-trigger-a-review).

## Run Locally

```bash
export OPENROUTER_API_KEY=sk-or-...

lgtmaybe review --provider openrouter --model anthropic/claude-sonnet-4.6
```

You can pass the key with `--api-key sk-or-...` instead of the env var. Either
way, the key is never persisted to config.

## Choosing the Model

OpenRouter models are named `vendor/model`. Pick whichever fits your budget and
quality bar, for example:

- `anthropic/claude-sonnet-4.6`
- `openai/gpt-5.5`
- `z-ai/glm-4.6`

Browse the full catalogue and per-model pricing at
<https://openrouter.ai/models>.

One catalogue quirk: a model can accept JSON-schema mode through OpenRouter yet
return replies that parse as empty, so the review comes back with zero findings
and no error (seen with `anthropic/claude-fable-5.1`). If a model is silent on
everything, try one diff with `--no-structured-output` (see
[Configure .lgtmaybe.yml](configure-lgtmaybe-yml.md#structured_output)) before
writing the model off.

## Credit Reservations

OpenRouter checks your balance before it generates anything, and it costs the
worst case: the prompt plus the most tokens the reply could use. A request with
no cap is assumed to want the model's full output ceiling, so a review can be
refused for credit it was never going to spend:

```
This request requires more credits, or fewer max_tokens.
You requested up to 65536 tokens, but can only afford 25905.
```

To keep that reservation realistic, OpenRouter reviews send a default cap of
16384 tokens per call. If a refusal names a larger number, something has
overridden the default. Check the `per-call budget resolved` log line, which
names the ceiling and where it came from:

```
per-call budget resolved  timeout_s=1800  max_tokens=16384  max_tokens_source="provider default"
```

Top up, or lower the cap so the reservation fits your balance:

```yaml
max_tokens: 8192
```

`--max-tokens 8192` does the same for one run, and `max_tokens` is also a GitHub
Action input. Lower it with care: a cap that is too low truncates the findings
JSON mid-object, and reasoning models spend this same budget on thinking tokens,
so they need more headroom than a plain model. `max_tokens: 0` removes the cap
and puts the reservation back to the model's full ceiling.

lgtmaybe treats this refusal as permanent and stops after one attempt. Your
balance cannot grow mid-review, so retrying every lens would only waste runner
time before reporting the same failure.

## Rate Limits

A capacity 429 is different: it is temporary, and lgtmaybe handles it for you.
Rate-limited calls back off on a 20s-60s ladder, long enough to reach a fresh
per-minute window, and honour OpenRouter's `Retry-After` header when it sends
one (clamped at 120s). A lens that is still failing on the provider when the
fan-out drains is re-run once more.

That rescue covers provider-side failures only. It leaves alone unparseable
output, a blown `max_tokens` ceiling, a batch the oversized-diff split already
retried, an unrecoverable failure such as a spent quota, and any limit you set
(`max_review_seconds`, `max_review_tokens`, a cancelled job), because a second
attempt would buy the same answer at full price. Usually you will see none of
this. A review that could not recover says so in its summary and names the lens
it lost.

If you are seeing rate limits, check the review's own burst before blaming the
model. Every `(batch, lens)` call shares one concurrency pool and one API key, so
a wide fan-out can throttle itself:

```yaml
max_concurrency: 3
```

Beyond that, it is a question about your OpenRouter account. Limits on free model
variants (the `:free` suffix) are account-wide rather than per-model, and the
daily allowance depends on how much credit the account has bought, so a review
is far more likely to be throttled on a free variant than a paid one. Paid
models carry no OpenRouter platform request cap, though the upstream provider
behind a model can still rate-limit you. Neither is the same as a per-key credit
spending cap, which limits what a key may spend, not how often it may call.

## Persist Non-Secret Defaults

Provider and model are not secrets, so they can live in `.lgtmaybe.yml`. The key
stays in the environment.

```yaml
provider: openrouter
model: anthropic/claude-sonnet-4.6
```

With that file in place, `lgtmaybe review` needs no flags. See
[Configure .lgtmaybe.yml](configure-lgtmaybe-yml.md) for every setting.

[wf]: https://github.com/MattJColes/lgtmaybe/blob/main/examples/workflows/review-openrouter.yml

---

# Review with z.ai (GLM)

[z.ai](https://z.ai/)'s GLM models (from Zhipu AI) are a first-class provider:
add a `ZAI_API_KEY` and pick a model. lgtmaybe reaches them through litellm's
native `zai/` route, so the international endpoint needs no `api_base`.

## Contents

- [Get an API key](#get-an-api-key)
- [GitHub Action](#github-action)
- [Run locally](#run-locally)
- [Choosing the model](#choosing-the-model)
- [China / coding-plan endpoint](#china-coding-plan-endpoint)
- [Persist non-secret defaults](#persist-non-secret-defaults)

## Get an API Key

Create a key in the [z.ai developer console](https://z.ai/) (see the
[API docs](https://docs.z.ai/)). In your repository, add it as an Actions secret
named `ZAI_API_KEY`
(**Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions → New repository secret**).

## GitHub Action

Copy [`examples/workflows/review-zai.yml`][wf] to
`.github/workflows/lgtmaybe.yml`. The core step is:

```yaml
- uses: MattJColes/lgtmaybe@v2
  with:
    provider: zai
    model: glm-4.6
    api_key: ${{ secrets.ZAI_API_KEY }}
```

The workflow runs on `pull_request_target`, so the secret is available, but PR
code is never checked out: lgtmaybe reads the diff through the API. See
[Use as a GitHub Action](use-as-github-action.md) for the full workflow,
including [who can trigger a review](use-as-github-action.md#who-can-trigger-a-review).

## Run Locally

```bash
export ZAI_API_KEY=...

lgtmaybe review --provider zai --model glm-4.6
```

You can pass the key with `--api-key ...` instead of the env var. Either way, the
key is never persisted to config.

## Choosing the Model

Pass any GLM chat model your key can access, such as `glm-4.6`, `glm-4.7`,
`glm-4.5-air`, or a newer `glm-5.x`. Use the name z.ai's API expects; lgtmaybe
adds the `zai/` route prefix for you.

## China / Coding-Plan Endpoint

The native route targets z.ai's international endpoint. To use the China or
coding-plan endpoint instead, point `--api-base` (or `ZAI_API_BASE`, or the
Action's `api_base` input) at it:

```bash
lgtmaybe review \
  --provider zai \
  --model glm-4.6 \
  --api-base https://open.bigmodel.cn/api/paas/v4
```

## Persist Non-Secret Defaults

Provider and model are not secrets, so they can live in `.lgtmaybe.yml`. The key
stays in the environment.

```yaml
provider: zai
model: glm-4.6
```

With that file in place, `lgtmaybe review` needs no flags. See
[Configure .lgtmaybe.yml](configure-lgtmaybe-yml.md) for every setting.
