# Review with AWS Bedrock (Keyless OIDC)

Use this guide to run lgtmaybe with AWS Bedrock using GitHub's OIDC token, so no
static AWS credentials are stored in secrets.

## Contents

- [How it works](#how-it-works)
- [One-time AWS setup](#one-time-aws-setup)
- [Workflow example](#workflow-example)
- [Choosing a Bedrock model ID](#choosing-a-bedrock-model-id)
- [Running locally with ambient AWS credentials](#running-locally-with-ambient-aws-credentials)
- [Troubleshooting](#troubleshooting)

## How It Works

GitHub Actions issues a short-lived OIDC token. AWS STS exchanges it for
temporary credentials for an IAM role you control. Pass `aws_role_arn` and the
Action performs that exchange for you; lgtmaybe then picks up the credentials
through the standard AWS credential chain. There is no `AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID` or
`AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY` in your secrets.

## One-Time AWS Setup

Do this once in your AWS account:

1. Create an IAM OIDC identity provider for `token.actions.githubusercontent.com`.
2. Create an IAM role with a trust policy scoped to your repository
   (`repo:<org>/<repo>:*`).
3. Attach the least-privilege policy below.
4. Confirm the models you want are enabled in the target region (model access
   in the Bedrock console).
5. Note the role ARN (e.g. `arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/lgtmaybe-bedrock`).
   It becomes the `aws_role_arn` Action input.

The role needs only:

```json
{
  "Effect": "Allow",
  "Action": [
    "bedrock:InvokeModel",
    "bedrock:InvokeModelWithResponseStream"
  ],
  "Resource": [
    "arn:aws:bedrock:*:<account-id>:inference-profile/*",
    "arn:aws:bedrock:*::foundation-model/*"
  ]
}
```

Both ARNs are required for the recommended inference-profile model IDs (the
`us.`/`eu.`/`apac.`-prefixed IDs below). A cross-region inference profile routes
the call to the foundation model in several regions, so the role needs
`bedrock:InvokeModel*` on both the `inference-profile/*` ARN and the underlying
`foundation-model/*` ARN. Granting only one still fails with
`AccessDeniedException`. A bare `anthropic.…` model ID needs only the
`foundation-model/*` ARN, but most current Claude models can only be invoked
through an inference profile (see the model table below).

Once it works, scope each `Resource` to specific model and inference-profile
ARNs for tighter least privilege, e.g.
`arn:aws:bedrock:*:<account-id>:inference-profile/us.anthropic.claude-opus-5-5*`
and `arn:aws:bedrock:*::foundation-model/anthropic.claude-opus-5-5*`.

## Workflow Example

Copy [`examples/workflows/review-bedrock.yml`][wf] to
`.github/workflows/lgtmaybe.yml` and store the role ARN in an `AWS_ROLE_ARN`
secret. The Action assumes the role itself, so you need no separate
`configure-aws-credentials` step, but the workflow must grant `id-token: write`
so GitHub will mint the OIDC token:

```yaml
permissions:
  contents: read
  pull-requests: write
  id-token: write # required for the OIDC token exchange (keyless auth)
```

The review step is:

```yaml
- uses: MattJColes/lgtmaybe@v2
  with:
    provider: bedrock
    model: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-6
    aws_role_arn: ${{ secrets.AWS_ROLE_ARN }}
    aws_region: us-east-1
```

`aws_region` defaults to `us-east-1`. The example also carries the
trusted-author guard described in
[who can trigger a review](use-as-github-action.md#who-can-trigger-a-review).

## Choosing a Bedrock Model ID

The `model` must be a Bedrock model identifier. Bedrock hosts Anthropic Claude,
Amazon Nova, Meta Llama, Mistral, Cohere, OpenAI GPT and others, each under
Bedrock's own ID: `openai.gpt-6-sol`, not OpenAI's `gpt-6-sol`. An ID written
for another provider's API is rejected with
`The provided model identifier is invalid`. Use one of the Claude IDs below:

| Model | Inference-profile ID (recommended) | Base model ID |
|---|---|---|
| Claude Opus 5.5 | `us.anthropic.claude-opus-5-5` | `anthropic.claude-opus-5-5` |
| Claude Sonnet 4.6 | `us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-6` | `anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-6` |
| Claude Haiku 4.5 | `us.anthropic.claude-haiku-4-5-20251001-v1:0` | `anthropic.claude-haiku-4-5-20251001-v1:0` |

Haiku 4.5 keeps its dated `-20251001-v1:0` suffix on Bedrock; unlike Opus 5.5
and Sonnet 4.6, it has no undated `anthropic.claude-haiku-4-5` ID.

On Bedrock, Claude Opus 4.7 and later (Opus 5.5 included) take lgtmaybe's
findings schema as a forced tool call rather than native structured output.
litellm picks that route from its model map, so there is nothing to configure.

Prefer the inference-profile form. Most current Claude models on Bedrock can
only be invoked through a cross-region inference profile, not with on-demand
throughput on the bare model ID, so a bare ID often fails with the same
`invalid model identifier` (or `on-demand throughput isn't supported`) error.
Prefix the ID with the geography that matches `aws_region`: `us.` (US), `eu.`
(Europe) or `apac.` (Asia Pacific), or the narrower `au.` / `jp.`. A `global.`
prefix lets Bedrock route the call to any commercial region. Use the bare
`anthropic.…` ID only where on-demand access to that model is enabled in your
region.

## Running Locally with Ambient AWS Credentials

If your shell has AWS credentials (from `~/.aws`, SSO, or an assumed role), you
can review your current branch with Bedrock. Bedrock request signing needs
`boto3`, so install the `bedrock` extra (the Action image already bundles it):

```bash
pip install 'lgtmaybe[bedrock]'

lgtmaybe review \
  --provider bedrock \
  --model us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-6
```

Bedrock always uses the AWS credential chain; lgtmaybe ignores `--api-key` for
it.

> **`No matching distribution found for lgtmaybe[bedrock]`** (`from versions:
> none`): this is not a packaging problem, because the `bedrock` extra is
> published on PyPI. `pip` found no version compatible with your environment.
> The usual cause is a Python older than the required 3.11 (check with
> `python --version`), so install under 3.11 or later (e.g. with `pipx` or `uv`).
> If your Python is fine, `pip` can't reach PyPI: check your network, proxy or
> `--index-url`.

## Troubleshooting

**`ExpiredTokenException`**: the OIDC exchange failed or the role session
expired. Check that the workflow grants `id-token: write` and that the IAM trust
policy names the correct GitHub repository.

**`AccessDeniedException`**: the role lacks `bedrock:InvokeModel` for the
selected model, or the model is not enabled in the Bedrock console for your
account and region. For an inference-profile ID (`us.`/`eu.`/`apac.`-prefixed),
the policy must allow the `inference-profile/*` ARN as well as
`foundation-model/*`.

**`The provided model identifier is invalid`**: the `model` is not a Bedrock
model ID. Either it is another provider's name (such as `gpt-6-sol` or
`claude-sonnet-4-6`; Bedrock's are `openai.gpt-6-sol` and
`us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-6`), so pick an ID from the table above, or the
model needs a cross-region inference profile, so prefix it with
`us.`/`eu.`/`apac.` (e.g. `us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-6`) instead of using the
bare `anthropic.…` ID.

**`output_config.format: Extra inputs are not permitted`**, **`outputConfig`**,
or a `toolConfig` / "doesn't support tool choice" refusal: the model's Converse
route doesn't accept the structured-output shape lgtmaybe sent, and Bedrock
rejected the request with a 400. No action is needed. lgtmaybe re-sends the same
schema as a forced tool call (which Converse does implement) and the rest of the
lens fan-out uses that shape straight away. Only a route that refuses the tool
call too falls back to prompt-instructed JSON, which the lenient parser still
reads; that fallback is logged as a warning naming the model and the reason. If
every lens fails at once with `every review call failed` on an older lgtmaybe,
upgrade, or pass `--no-structured-output` (`structured_output: false`) as a
stopgap.

**Structured output stepped down after an odd reply**: an empty reply, or one
that parsed to something other than findings, moves the model one rung down to
the forced tool call and keeps the schema. Only a second such reply gives the
schema up. The provider log says which happened:
`structured output stepped down to a forced tool call` is the middle rung and
costs nothing, while `structured output disabled for this model` is the floor
and carries a `reason` (such as `rejected`, `empty-response`,
`unparseable-output`, `tool-rejected` or `internal-tool-rejected`) worth
reading.

[wf]: https://github.com/MattJColes/lgtmaybe/blob/main/examples/workflows/review-bedrock.yml

---

<!-- Source: https://lgtmaybe.coles.codes/how-to/review-with-vertex-wif/ -->

# Review with Google Vertex AI (Keyless WIF)

Use this guide to run lgtmaybe with Google Vertex AI using Workload Identity
Federation (WIF), so no service-account JSON or static key is stored in secrets.

## Contents

- [How it works](#how-it-works)
- [One-time GCP setup](#one-time-gcp-setup)
- [Workflow example](#workflow-example)
- [Environment variables](#environment-variables)
- [Available Vertex AI models](#available-vertex-ai-models)
- [Running locally with ADC](#running-locally-with-adc)
- [Troubleshooting](#troubleshooting)

## How It Works

GitHub Actions issues an OIDC token. WIF exchanges it for a short-lived GCP
access token that impersonates a service account holding only the Vertex AI
permissions it needs. lgtmaybe picks up those credentials through Application
Default Credentials (ADC).

## One-Time GCP Setup

Do this once in your GCP project:

1. Enable the Vertex AI API on the project.
2. Create a workload identity pool and a GitHub provider in it.
3. Create a service account with `roles/aiplatform.user`, or something narrower.
   That role grants `aiplatform.endpoints.predict`; do not assign broader
   project-level roles.
4. Grant the GitHub principal permission to impersonate that service account,
   scoped to your repository.
5. Note the WIF provider resource name (for `gcp_wif_provider`) and the service
   account email (for `gcp_service_account`).

## Workflow Example

Copy [`examples/workflows/review-vertex.yml`][wf] to
`.github/workflows/lgtmaybe.yml` and store the provider resource name and service
account email in `GCP_WIF_PROVIDER` and `GCP_SERVICE_ACCOUNT` secrets. The Action
authenticates to GCP itself, so you need no separate
`google-github-actions/auth` step, but the workflow must grant `id-token: write`:

```yaml
permissions:
  contents: read
  pull-requests: write
  id-token: write # required for the WIF token exchange (keyless auth)
```

The review step is:

```yaml
- uses: MattJColes/lgtmaybe@v2
  with:
    provider: vertex
    model: gemini-3.8-flash
    gcp_wif_provider: ${{ secrets.GCP_WIF_PROVIDER }}
    gcp_service_account: ${{ secrets.GCP_SERVICE_ACCOUNT }}
```

The example also carries the trusted-author guard described in
[who can trigger a review](use-as-github-action.md#who-can-trigger-a-review).

## Environment Variables

litellm reads the project and region from these variables:

| Variable | Required | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `VERTEXAI_PROJECT` | No | GCP project ID. Defaults to the project your ADC resolves (`GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT`, or your gcloud config). |
| `VERTEXAI_LOCATION` | No | Region (default: `us-central1`) |

In the Action, the authentication step sets the project for you. The Action
forwards only `GOOGLE_*` and `CLOUDSDK_*` variables (plus `AWS_*`, `AZURE_*` and
its own `INPUT_*`) into its container, so `VERTEXAI_*` variables set in your
workflow do not reach lgtmaybe there. The Action therefore always uses
litellm's default region, `us-central1`; to use another region, run the CLI in
a workflow step with `VERTEXAI_LOCATION` set instead.

## Available Vertex AI Models

| Model | Vertex model ID |
|---|---|
| Gemini 3.8 Flash | `gemini-3.8-flash` |
| Gemini 3.5 Flash | `gemini-3.5-flash` |
| Gemini 3.1 Pro (preview) | `gemini-3.1-pro-preview` |
| Gemini 3 Pro (preview) | `gemini-3-pro-preview` |
| Gemini 2.5 Pro | `gemini-2.5-pro` |
| Claude Opus 5.5 | `claude-opus-5-5` |

Use the Gemini 3.x Pro `-preview` IDs as written: litellm's model map has no
bare `gemini-3-pro` or `gemini-3.1-pro` entry, so with those lgtmaybe can't fit
its input budget to the model's window. Claude on Vertex must be enabled in
Model Garden first, and `VERTEXAI_LOCATION` must be a region that serves it.

## Running Locally with ADC

Sign in with `gcloud auth application-default login` so your shell has ADC.
Vertex token minting needs `google-auth`, so install the `vertex` extra (the
Action image already bundles it):

```bash
pip install 'lgtmaybe[vertex]'

export VERTEXAI_PROJECT=my-project
export VERTEXAI_LOCATION=us-central1

lgtmaybe review \
  --provider vertex \
  --model gemini-3.8-flash
```

This reviews your current branch with Vertex. Vertex always uses ambient
credentials; lgtmaybe ignores `--api-key` for it.

## Troubleshooting

**`vertex requires ambient GCP credentials`**: lgtmaybe found no sign of GCP
credentials (`GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS`, a project variable such as
`GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT` or `VERTEXAI_PROJECT`, the ADC file gcloud writes, or
metadata-server credentials, which need the `google-auth` package). Run `gcloud auth application-default login`, set
`GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS`, or (in CI) check the WIF inputs.

**`UNAUTHENTICATED`**: ADC credentials are missing or expired. Run
`gcloud auth application-default login` locally, or check the WIF provider and
the service account impersonation binding in CI.

**`PERMISSION_DENIED`**: the service account lacks `roles/aiplatform.user`, or
the Vertex AI API is not enabled in the project. Enable it with:

```bash
gcloud services enable aiplatform.googleapis.com --project=my-project
```

**`Model not found`**: the model ID may not be available in your selected
region. Check the [Vertex AI Model Garden](https://console.cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/model-garden).

[wf]: https://github.com/MattJColes/lgtmaybe/blob/main/examples/workflows/review-vertex.yml

---

<!-- Source: https://lgtmaybe.coles.codes/how-to/review-with-azure/ -->

# Review with Azure OpenAI (Keyless OIDC)

Use this guide to run lgtmaybe against Azure OpenAI with GitHub's OIDC token
federated to Entra (Azure AD), so no static Azure key is stored in secrets. A
key-based alternative is covered at the end.

## Contents

- [How it works](#how-it-works)
- [One-time Azure setup](#one-time-azure-setup)
- [Workflow example](#workflow-example)
- [Choosing the model name](#choosing-the-model-name)
- [Running locally with ambient Azure credentials](#running-locally-with-ambient-azure-credentials)
- [Key-based alternative](#key-based-alternative)
- [Troubleshooting](#troubleshooting)

## How It Works

GitHub Actions issues a short-lived OIDC token. Entra exchanges it for an access
token for your Azure OpenAI resource, through a federated credential on an app
registration or managed identity. Pass `azure_client_id` and `azure_tenant_id`
and the Action sets up that exchange for you; lgtmaybe then picks up the token
through `azure-identity`'s `DefaultAzureCredential`. There is no
`AZURE_API_KEY` in your secrets.

Azure still needs two non-secret values: the deployment name (`model`) and the
resource endpoint (`api_base`, `https://<resource>.openai.azure.com`).

## One-Time Azure Setup

Do this once in your Azure tenant:

1. Register an Entra app (or use a user-assigned managed identity). Note its
   client ID (`azure_client_id`) and your tenant ID (`azure_tenant_id`).
2. Add a federated credential to it for GitHub Actions:
   - Issuer: `https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com`
   - Subject: scoped to your repo, e.g. `repo:<org>/<repo>:pull_request`
     (or `:ref:refs/heads/main`, `:environment:…`)
   - Audience: `api://AzureADTokenExchange`
3. On the Azure OpenAI resource, grant the app the
   **Cognitive Services OpenAI User** role. It is least privilege: it can call
   models but not manage the resource.
4. Deploy the model you want and note the deployment name. That is what you
   pass as `model`, not the upstream OpenAI model ID.
5. Note the resource endpoint (`https://<resource>.openai.azure.com`). It
   becomes `api_base`.

## Workflow Example

Copy [`examples/workflows/review-azure.yml`][wf] to
`.github/workflows/lgtmaybe.yml` and set the `AZURE_CLIENT_ID`,
`AZURE_TENANT_ID` and `AZURE_API_BASE` secrets. The Action performs the OIDC
exchange itself, so you need no separate `azure/login` step, but the workflow
must grant `id-token: write` so GitHub will mint the token:

```yaml
permissions:
  id-token: write          # required for the OIDC token exchange (keyless)
  contents: read
  pull-requests: write
```

The review step is:

```yaml
- uses: MattJColes/lgtmaybe@v2
  with:
    provider: azure
    model: my-gpt-4o-deployment      # your Azure deployment name
    api_base: ${{ secrets.AZURE_API_BASE }}  # https://<resource>.openai.azure.com
    azure_client_id: ${{ secrets.AZURE_CLIENT_ID }}
    azure_tenant_id: ${{ secrets.AZURE_TENANT_ID }}
```

The example also carries the trusted-author guard described in
[who can trigger a review](use-as-github-action.md#who-can-trigger-a-review).

## Choosing the Model Name

For Azure, `model` is the deployment name you chose in the portal, not the
underlying OpenAI model ID. A deployment of `gpt-4o` named `my-gpt-4o-deployment`
is referenced as `model: my-gpt-4o-deployment`, which litellm routes as
`azure/my-gpt-4o-deployment`.

## Running Locally with Ambient Azure Credentials

Keyless works locally too. Install the `azure` extra, sign in (or use a managed
identity), set the endpoint, and review your current branch:

```bash
pip install 'lgtmaybe[azure]'
az login

export AZURE_API_BASE="https://<resource>.openai.azure.com"

lgtmaybe review \
  --provider azure \
  --model my-gpt-4o-deployment
```

`DefaultAzureCredential` finds your `az login` session (or a managed identity,
or `AZURE_*` env vars), and no static key is stored.

## Key-Based Alternative

To use a resource key instead, pass it as `api_key` with the endpoint as
`api_base`. Drop `azure_client_id`, `azure_tenant_id` and the `id-token`
permission. A supplied key always wins over ambient credentials, and the
`azure-identity` package is not needed in this mode.

```yaml
- uses: MattJColes/lgtmaybe@v2
  with:
    provider: azure
    model: my-gpt-4o-deployment
    api_key: ${{ secrets.AZURE_API_KEY }}
    api_base: ${{ secrets.AZURE_API_BASE }}
```

Locally, `export AZURE_API_KEY=… AZURE_API_BASE=…` (or pass `--api-key` and
`--api-base`).

## Troubleshooting

**`azure requires credentials`**: lgtmaybe found neither a key nor an ambient
Entra credential. For keyless, check that `id-token: write` is present and the
federated credential's subject matches the triggering ref or event. For key
mode, set `AZURE_API_KEY` (or the `api_key` input).

**`azure requires the resource endpoint`**: set `api_base` (or `AZURE_API_BASE`)
to `https://<resource>.openai.azure.com`.

**`keyless azure needs the azure-identity package`**: you are running keyless on
the CLI without the extra. Install `lgtmaybe[azure]`. The Action image already
bundles it.

**`AADSTS70021` / no matching federated identity**: the federated credential's
issuer, subject or audience don't match this workflow. The audience must be
`api://AzureADTokenExchange` and the subject must match the repo and event.

**`DeploymentNotFound` / 404**: `model` must be the deployment name on the
resource that `api_base` points at, not the upstream OpenAI model ID.

**`Unsupported API version`**: pin one by setting `AZURE_API_VERSION` (e.g.
`2024-08-01-preview`) in the environment. Otherwise litellm uses its default.

[wf]: https://github.com/MattJColes/lgtmaybe/blob/main/examples/workflows/review-azure.yml

---

<!-- Source: https://lgtmaybe.coles.codes/how-to/run-locally-with-ollama/ -->

# Run Locally with ollama

Use this guide to review your local changes with a local ollama model: no API
cost, no egress, no keys. The CLI reviews your `git` diff and prints the
findings. To post reviews on pull requests, use the
[GitHub Action](use-as-github-action.md).

> **ollama is the easiest local start.** Running a different local server
> (vLLM, llama.cpp or LM Studio) or a hosted OpenAI-compatible API like
> DeepSeek? Use the `openai-compatible` provider instead:
> [Other OpenAI-compatible servers](use-a-custom-openai-compatible-endpoint.md).
> The [model-choice and hardware guidance below](#which-model-and-will-it-fit)
> applies to any local runtime.

## Contents

- [Prerequisites](#prerequisites)
- [Pull the model you want](#pull-the-model-you-want)
- [Which model, and will it fit?](#which-model-and-will-it-fit)
- [Run the review](#run-the-review)
- [Reviewing large files (recursive walk)](#reviewing-large-files-recursive-walk)
- [Use a remote ollama instance](#use-a-remote-ollama-instance)
- [Inside the GitHub Action's container](#inside-the-github-actions-container)
- [Get findings as JSON](#get-findings-as-json)
- [Let an AI agent apply the fixes](#let-an-ai-agent-apply-the-fixes)
- [Concurrency on a local server](#concurrency-on-a-local-server)
- [The output ceiling (why a review can't run forever)](#the-output-ceiling-why-a-review-cant-run-forever)
- [Slow models and timeouts](#slow-models-and-timeouts)
- [Troubleshooting](#troubleshooting)

## Prerequisites

- lgtmaybe installed (`pip install lgtmaybe`)
- [ollama](https://ollama.com) installed and running
- A local git repository with changes to review

## Pull the Model You Want

```bash
ollama pull qwen3.6:27b        # strong all-round coding model
ollama pull gemma4:e4b         # smaller, for devices with limited RAM
```

List the models you have:

```bash
ollama list
```

## Which Model, and Will It Fit?

Two rules:

1. **Pick a coding model.** Reviewing a PR is a coding task, so use a model
   built for code (e.g. the Qwen3 coder line), not a general chat model.
2. **Bigger and newer is more accurate.** Use the largest, most recent coding
   model your hardware can run. Our accuracy numbers are for a small model: we
   benchmarked `qwen3.5:4b`, and it did well, but only with recursive review on
   (88% vs 61% recall). A larger, newer model catches more and relies on that
   less.

A solid mid-2026 default is Qwen3.6-27B (`qwen3.6:27b`). It is close to frontier
API models on coding benchmarks (SWE-bench Verified ~77%) yet small enough for a
workstation or a well-specced laptop, so it clears lgtmaybe's bar across all the
review lenses without a data-centre GPU. Smaller models work too, but accuracy
falls off: you will miss subtler findings and may need `--no-reflect`, because
the reflection pass over-prunes on a weak model.

**Hardware, quantised (the usual way to run it locally):**

| You have | What to expect |
|---|---|
| **< 32 GB** RAM/VRAM | Drop to a smaller model (`gemma4:e4b`) or use a hosted provider. 27B at a usable quant won't leave room for the diff. |
| **32 GB** RAM/VRAM | The practical floor. Run `qwen3.6:27b` at a 4-bit quant (≈16-18 GB of weights) with a modest context window. Keep `num_ctx` conservative so the model plus the diff and findings fit. |
| **48 GB+** RAM/VRAM (preferred) | Comfortable. Room for the weights plus the default `--num-ctx` (32k), or a raised 64k window for very large diffs, with headroom for the KV cache. |

This applies to discrete VRAM and Apple Silicon unified memory alike. A bigger
context window costs memory on top of the weights, so if you raise `--num-ctx`
for a large diff (see [Slow models and timeouts](#slow-models-and-timeouts)),
size it to the table above. On a hosted provider none of this matters: the model
runs on the provider's hardware.

## Run the Review

From inside the repository, on the branch you want reviewed:

```bash
lgtmaybe review \
  --provider ollama \
  --model qwen3.6:27b \
  --api-base http://localhost:11434
```

`http://localhost:11434` is the default, so `--api-base` is optional here.

This diffs your current branch against the remote primary branch and prints the
findings. Add `--working` to review the whole worktree (branch commits plus
uncommitted edits) against that same base, `--uncommitted` to review only your
uncommitted edits against HEAD, or `--base <ref>` to diff against a different
base.

## Reviewing Large Files (Recursive Walk)

When a single file's diff is larger than the per-call token budget
(`--max-input-tokens`), lgtmaybe walks it hunk by hunk, reviewing each hunk in
its own focused call, instead of sending the whole file and letting the tail drop
out of the model's attention. The findings are merged, and inline-comment
positions still bind to the real diff. This recursive (RLM-style) review is on
by default (`recursive: true`). Files that fit the budget are still reviewed
whole, so nothing changes for small diffs.

It helps small local models most, because a smaller prompt is easier to review
thoroughly. In our A/B benchmark a local `qwen3.5:4b` caught all 6 planted bugs
reviewing recursively, versus 4 of 6 reviewing each file whole. The two it
missed were both in the file's tail, even though the diff fit the context window,
so the gain is focus, not just avoiding truncation. It is a single
non-deterministic run on one fixture, so treat it as directional; the harness is
described in
[DEVELOPMENT.md](https://github.com/MattJColes/lgtmaybe/blob/main/DEVELOPMENT.md#benchmarking-the-recursive-rlm-walk).

To review each file whole instead (one call per file, which keeps all of a
file's hunks in view together but tends to miss more on big files with small
models), pass `--no-recursive`:

```bash
lgtmaybe review --provider ollama --model qwen3.5:4b \
  --api-base http://localhost:11434 --no-recursive
```

```yaml
# or in .lgtmaybe.yml (also how the GitHub Action picks it up):
recursive: false
```

## Use a Remote ollama Instance

If ollama runs on another machine (e.g. a Tailscale peer):

```bash
lgtmaybe review \
  --provider ollama \
  --model qwen3.6:27b \
  --api-base http://100.x.x.x:11434
```

lgtmaybe adds no authentication, and ollama has none built in, so restrict
network access at the host or firewall.

## Inside the GitHub Action's Container

The Action runs lgtmaybe in a container, so an ollama server on the runner host
is reached at `host.docker.internal`, not `localhost`. Set it with the Action's
`provider`, `model` and `api_base` inputs, or in `.lgtmaybe.yml`:

```yaml
provider: ollama
model: qwen3.6:27b
api_base: http://host.docker.internal:11434
```

## Get Findings as JSON

The CLI prints a readable listing by default and never posts anywhere. Add
`--json` for a machine-readable array you can pipe into other tools:

```bash
lgtmaybe review \
  --provider ollama \
  --model qwen3.6:27b \
  --api-base http://localhost:11434 \
  --json
```

## Let an AI Agent Apply the Fixes

`--format agent` prints the findings as correction instructions an AI coding
agent (such as Claude Code) can read and apply, so you can review and fix a
branch locally before opening a PR. See
[Fix findings with an AI agent](fix-findings-with-an-ai-agent.md).

## Concurrency on a Local Server

lgtmaybe fans its review calls out across a pool sized by `max_concurrency`,
6 by default on every provider, local included. That is a ceiling on what
lgtmaybe will have in flight, not a promise that your server runs them at once:

- **A default ollama runs one request at a time.** `OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL` is `1`
  unless you set it, so five of six calls queue (up to `OLLAMA_MAX_QUEUE`, 512).
  Nothing is lost and nothing fails; the wall clock is your server's throughput
  either way. Raising `max_concurrency` alone changes nothing.
- **The setting that matters is on the server.** Start ollama with
  `OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL=4` and four calls really do run together.
- **It costs memory in proportion.** ollama allocates the context window per
  parallel slot: four slots at `num_ctx` 32768 need 128k of context, not 32k.
  This is the usual reason a machine that reviewed happily with one slot falls
  over with four.

So the two settings should match. If you have raised the server, tell lgtmaybe:

```bash
lgtmaybe review --max-concurrency 4
```

**How to tell which you got.** `--profile` answers it: compare the per-call
`elapsed` column with the `review` stage total. If the calls' elapsed times sum
to roughly the stage time, they ran one after another; if they sum to well over
it, they overlapped.

```
review             95.32s        <- stage total
correctness         52.02s   |
spec                45.64s   |   sum is ~3x the stage,
artefacts           43.67s   |   so these overlapped
security            43.30s   |
```

**Queue time is already covered.** A queued call's timeout clock starts when the
request is sent, not when your server gets to it, so on a single-slot server the
last call in a six-wide fan-out would otherwise have to finish within the same
budget as the first. lgtmaybe scales the local default timeout by the fan-out
width to cover that (see [below](#slow-models-and-timeouts)), so you should not
need to intervene. If you would rather the calls didn't queue at all:

```yaml
# .lgtmaybe.yml
max_concurrency: 1
```

## The Output Ceiling (Why a Review Can't Run Forever)

A local model under structured output sometimes fails to stop and keeps
decoding. With no ceiling, only the per-call timeout ends it: half an hour of
sustained GPU for a single lens on a one-file diff, and hours for a whole review.

So a review runs with a default output ceiling of 16384 tokens per call, half
the default 32768 `num_ctx`. Measured findings payloads are hundreds of tokens,
so the rest is headroom for a thinking model, which draws its reasoning from the
same budget.

The same ceiling applies to `openai-compatible` and `openrouter`, because the
failure is not specific to local models: benchmarking found a model behind
`openai-compatible` emitting 223,558 tokens on a single lens call, and a hosted
model on `openrouter` returning a 393k-token response that parsed into 699 false
positives on a diff with nothing wrong in it. The first-party APIs (openai,
anthropic, zai, bedrock, vertex, azure) get no default ceiling, because they have
not shown this failure and a cap could truncate long findings payloads.

The ceiling is a fixed number, not a fraction of your window: raising `num_ctx`
for a big diff adds room for the prompt, not for a longer answer. Use
`max_tokens` when you want a longer answer.

Every run logs the ceiling it resolved and where it came from:

```
per-call budget resolved  timeout_s=3600  max_tokens=16384  max_tokens_source="provider default"
```

If a lens hits it, you get a truncation notice, not a silent clean review:

```
response hit the 16384-token `max_tokens` ceiling before finishing — the batch
is re-reviewed in smaller pieces automatically, so a lens that keeps doing it is
usually generation instability in the model, which a higher ceiling makes more
expensive rather than prevents
```

**One truncation is not a reason to raise the cap.** The batch is re-reviewed in
smaller pieces on its own, so a lens that trips it occasionally has still been
reviewed. A model that runs away repeatedly is generating past the ceiling, not
being cut short by it. A bigger ceiling only makes a longer wasted call; changing
the model is what fixes it.

Raising it is right when a genuinely long answer is being cut off: a large diff
with many real findings, where most are salvaged each time. Then raise it, or
remove the cap with `0`, which leaves the timeout as the run's only stop:

```bash
lgtmaybe review --provider ollama --model qwen3.5:4b --max-tokens 32768
lgtmaybe review --provider ollama --model qwen3.5:4b --max-tokens 0  # uncapped
```

```yaml
# or in .lgtmaybe.yml (also how the GitHub Action picks it up):
max_tokens: 32768
```

Lowering the ceiling is the quickest way to get a result out of a slow model:
`--max-tokens 512` turns a stuck review into one that finishes in minutes and
reports what it truncated.

## Slow Models and Timeouts

Local models are slow, especially large ones on CPU, so ollama gets a long
default per-call timeout of 1800 seconds. You don't need to set anything for a
normal run. (Direct cloud providers default to 600 seconds.)

**That default scales with the fan-out.** Because the calls queue, the budget
has to cover the wait as well as the work. At the default width of six the
per-call timeout is `1800 × 6`, bounded by `max_review_seconds` (3600 seconds by
default; `0` disables the deadline and with it the bound). It is never trimmed
below ollama's own 1800 seconds, so a deadline set lower than that does not
shrink it. The bound applies to the budget, not the wall clock: the deadline
decides when a call may start, so a call that begins just inside it still runs
its full budget. At `max_concurrency: 1` there is no queue and the budget is the
plain 1800 seconds. Every run logs the number it resolved, and why:

```
per-call budget resolved  timeout_s=3600  timeout_source="provider default"  concurrency=6
```

An explicit `timeout` is never scaled: `timeout: 600` means 600 at any width.

If a big model still times out (you'll see
`litellm.Timeout: Connection timed out after 3600.0 seconds`), raise it
explicitly:

```bash
# CLI flag (seconds):
lgtmaybe review --provider ollama --model qwen3.6:35b \
  --api-base http://localhost:11434 --timeout 3600
```

```yaml
# or in .lgtmaybe.yml (also how the GitHub Action picks it up):
provider: ollama
model: qwen3.6:35b
timeout: 1800
```

The review makes five lens calls under the default `fast` preset (one per
category under `--preset full`). On a default ollama those queue rather than
overlap, so a slow model takes roughly `lens calls × per-call time`. That is why
`fast` is the default: five calls instead of one per category is the biggest
single local speed-up.

To go faster, narrow the lenses with `categories:` in `.lgtmaybe.yml` (e.g. just
`security` and `correctness`), use a smaller model, or give ollama more GPU. If
you have the VRAM to serve requests in parallel, raise `OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL` on
the ollama server as described [above](#concurrency-on-a-local-server): the same
five calls then overlap instead of queueing, close to a 5× wall-clock win with
`OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL=5`. Add
`--profile` to any run to see the per-call breakdown.

## Troubleshooting

**`Connection refused` on port 11434**: make sure `ollama serve` is running and
the `--api-base` URL is reachable.

**Model not found**: run `ollama pull <model>` before using it.

**`review incomplete — every review call failed`**: every lens call timed out or
returned output that wasn't valid JSON. Raise `--timeout`, try a model that
follows instructions more reliably, or check the `LITELLM_LOG=DEBUG` output for
the underlying error. lgtmaybe reports this and exits non-zero rather than
pretending the PR is clean.

For a large diff this can mean the prompt plus the findings don't fit in
ollama's context window, so the output is truncated. lgtmaybe runs ollama with a
32768-token context (`num_ctx`) and structured JSON output, which covers most
reviews.

lgtmaybe does not send ollama's `think` flag. ollama already turns thinking on
for a model that supports it and rejects the flag for one that does not, so
sending nothing is right for both.

For a big multi-file change, raise the context window with `--num-ctx` so the
whole diff and the findings fit. This is ollama-only; hosted providers manage
their context window server-side and ignore it:

```bash
# A large multi-file diff on a local model: more time and more context
# (32768 is already the default; go above it for very large diffs):
lgtmaybe review --provider ollama --model qwen3.6:35b \
  --api-base http://localhost:11434 --timeout 1800 --num-ctx 65536
```

```yaml
# or in .lgtmaybe.yml (also how the GitHub Action picks it up):
provider: ollama
model: qwen3.6:35b
timeout: 1800
num_ctx: 65536
```

`--num-ctx` needs enough RAM/VRAM on the ollama host, so size it to your
machine. The budget that decides when lgtmaybe splits a diff into separate model
calls is `--max-input-tokens`, which applies to any provider. Its default
(100000) is lowered automatically to fit the model's window; on ollama that is
`num_ctx` minus the output ceiling, so 16384 tokens at the defaults. Set it
explicitly to send a large diff in fewer calls, or lower it for a small-context
model. If a very large diff still truncates, narrow it with `include_paths` /
`exclude_paths` or a lower `max_files` in `.lgtmaybe.yml`, or run a model with a
bigger context window.

> **If you set `--max-input-tokens` yourself, keep it under `--num-ctx`.** The
> two are independent: `--max-input-tokens` caps each batch lgtmaybe sends,
> while `--num-ctx` is the window ollama allocates. An explicit value is used as
> given, not fitted. lgtmaybe also estimates tokens with a generic tokeniser and
> local models tokenise differently, so leave headroom: a batch budget well
> below the window (e.g. `--max-input-tokens 16000` with `--num-ctx 32768`)
> avoids ollama silently truncating the findings JSON, which otherwise shows up
> only as an unhelpful "review failed".

**Review is empty or truncated**: the diff may exceed the model's context
window. Add a path filter in `.lgtmaybe.yml` to shrink the diff, or lower
`max_files`.

---

<!-- Source: https://lgtmaybe.coles.codes/how-to/use-a-custom-openai-compatible-endpoint/ -->

# Local Models and Other OpenAI-Compatible Providers

Many model servers speak the OpenAI `/v1` wire format: local and self-hosted
runtimes like [vLLM][vllm], [llama.cpp][llamacpp] and [LM Studio][lmstudio],
plus hosted APIs like [DeepSeek][deepseek] and many proxies. The
`openai-compatible` provider points lgtmaybe at any of them: you supply the base
URL and, if the server wants one, a key.

Use this provider when the model you want is not in the built-in provider list.

> Some endpoints that could run through here have a first-class provider
> instead, which needs less setup: [z.ai / GLM](review-with-zai.md) (`zai`) and
> [ollama](run-locally-with-ollama.md) (`ollama`).

## Contents

- [Local models at a glance](#local-models-at-a-glance)
- [How it works](#how-it-works)
- [DeepSeek (hosted, keyed)](#deepseek-hosted-keyed)
- [llama.cpp (local, keyless)](#llamacpp-local-keyless)
- [LM Studio (local, keyless)](#lm-studio-local-keyless)
- [vLLM (local or self-hosted, keyless)](#vllm-local-or-self-hosted-keyless)
- [Concurrency: what each server can actually take](#concurrency-what-each-server-can-actually-take)
- [Persist it in `.lgtmaybe.yml`](#persist-it-in-lgtmaybeyml)
- [Gateways that don't support JSON mode (`response_format`)](#gateways-that-dont-support-json-mode-response_format)

## Local Models at a Glance

Run a model on your own hardware, with no cost, no key, and nothing leaving the
machine:

| Runtime | Provider | Key needed? | See |
|---|---|---|---|
| [ollama][ollama] | `ollama` (native) | No | [Run locally with ollama](run-locally-with-ollama.md) |
| [vLLM][vllm] | `openai-compatible` | No | [below](#vllm-local-or-self-hosted-keyless) |
| [llama.cpp][llamacpp] | `openai-compatible` | No | [below](#llamacpp-local-keyless) |
| [LM Studio][lmstudio] | `openai-compatible` | No | [below](#lm-studio-local-keyless) |

ollama has its own `--provider ollama` and [its own guide](run-locally-with-ollama.md).
vLLM, llama.cpp and LM Studio are reached through `openai-compatible` and their
local server's `--api-base`, as shown below.

**Which model, and will it fit?** The ollama guide's model-choice and hardware
advice applies to any local runtime: pick a coding model, prefer bigger and
newer, and size it to your RAM/VRAM. See
[Which model, and will it fit?](run-locally-with-ollama.md#which-model-and-will-it-fit).

## How It Works

`--provider openai-compatible` routes through litellm's OpenAI client but sends
requests to the `--api-base` you give instead of `api.openai.com`. The base URL
is required (`--api-base` or `OPENAI_COMPATIBLE_API_BASE`); the API key is
optional:

- **Hosted endpoints** (DeepSeek, a paid proxy) need a key. Pass `--api-key` or
  set `OPENAI_COMPATIBLE_API_KEY`.
- **Local servers** (llama.cpp, LM Studio, vLLM) usually need none. lgtmaybe
  then sends a harmless placeholder key, because the OpenAI client rejects an
  empty one.

A key you supply is read from the environment or `--api-key` and is never
persisted to config.

Because the endpoint might be a slow local model, `openai-compatible` gets the
same generous 1800-second per-call timeout as ollama (scaled for queueing, see
[Concurrency](#concurrency-what-each-server-can-actually-take)), and the same
default output ceiling of 16384 tokens per call. For a fast hosted endpoint like
DeepSeek you can lower the timeout with `--timeout` (or `timeout:` in config).

## DeepSeek (Hosted, Keyed)

```bash
export OPENAI_COMPATIBLE_API_KEY=sk-...        # your DeepSeek key

lgtmaybe review \
  --provider openai-compatible \
  --model deepseek-chat \
  --api-base https://api.deepseek.com/v1
```

You can pass the key with `--api-key sk-...` instead of the env var.

## llama.cpp (Local, Keyless)

Start the server:

```bash
llama-server -m ./model.gguf --port 8000        # serves the OpenAI API at /v1
```

Then review against it, with no key:

```bash
lgtmaybe review \
  --provider openai-compatible \
  --model local-model \
  --api-base http://localhost:8000/v1
```

## LM Studio (Local, Keyless)

Enable the local server in LM Studio (it serves the OpenAI API on port `1234` by
default), then:

```bash
lgtmaybe review \
  --provider openai-compatible \
  --model your-loaded-model \
  --api-base http://localhost:1234/v1
```

## vLLM (Local or Self-Hosted, Keyless)

```bash
vllm serve meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct --port 8000
```

```bash
lgtmaybe review \
  --provider openai-compatible \
  --model meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct \
  --api-base http://localhost:8000/v1
```

## Concurrency: What Each Server Can Actually Take

lgtmaybe fans out across a pool sized by `max_concurrency`, 6 by default on
every provider. That is a ceiling on what it will have in flight; whether your
server runs the calls together is up to the server, and the three above differ
sharply:

| Server | Concurrent by default? | Raising it |
|---|---|---|
| **vLLM** | Yes, continuous batching | Close to free; each request keeps the full `--max-model-len` |
| **llama.cpp** | No, one slot | `-np N` adds slots, but **splits one KV cache between them** |
| **LM Studio** | No, single slot | Not exposed; set `max_concurrency` to 1 |

The llama.cpp trap fails as a quality problem rather than an error. `-np`
divides the context you asked for: `-c 32768 -np 4` leaves each slot 8k, and a
lgtmaybe review prompt is comfortably larger than that, so the diff is silently
truncated and the model reviews something it was never fully shown. Size `-c` as
`slots × per-slot context`:

```bash
llama-server -m ./model.gguf --port 8000 -np 4 -c 131072   # 4 slots × 32k each
```

vLLM allocates KV blocks dynamically rather than up front, so concurrent
requests each keep the full `--max-model-len`. That makes it the local server to
choose when review latency matters:

```bash
vllm serve <model> --port 8000 --max-model-len 32768
lgtmaybe review --provider openai-compatible --model <model> \
  --api-base http://localhost:8000/v1 --max-concurrency 6
```

**Queueing does not cost you a timeout.** A queued request's clock starts when it
is sent, not when a slot frees, so lgtmaybe scales the `openai-compatible`
default timeout (1800 seconds) by the fan-out width: `1800 × 6` at the default,
bounded by `max_review_seconds` (3600 seconds; `0` disables the deadline and the
bound with it). It is never trimmed below the 1800-second provider default, so a
deadline set lower than that does not shrink it. The bound applies to the budget,
not the wall clock: the deadline gates when a call may start, and does not cut a
running call short. An explicit `timeout` is used exactly as written, at any
width. Each run logs the number it resolved and the width it assumed:

```
per-call budget resolved  timeout_s=3600  timeout_source="provider default"  concurrency=6
```

For a single-slot server, you can say so and have lgtmaybe queue nothing:

```yaml
# .lgtmaybe.yml
max_concurrency: 1
```

## Persist It in `.lgtmaybe.yml`

The provider, model and base URL are not secrets, so they can live in config.
The key stays in the environment.

```yaml
provider: openai-compatible
model: deepseek-chat
api_base: https://api.deepseek.com/v1
```

With that file in place, `lgtmaybe review` needs no flags. In the GitHub Action,
set the same values as inputs (or in `.lgtmaybe.yml`) and pass `api_key` from a
secret for hosted endpoints; see
[`examples/workflows/review-openai-compatible.yml`][wf]. Leave `api_key` empty for
a keyless server on the runner host, reached from the Action's container at
`http://host.docker.internal:<port>/v1`.

## Gateways That Don't Support JSON Mode (`response_format`)

To keep models returning clean findings instead of prose, lgtmaybe asks for
structured output through the OpenAI `response_format` parameter (JSON mode).
Most endpoints honour it. Some enterprise gateways and custom proxies don't:
they either ignore it, so the model answers with the JSON in a ```` ```json ````
fence or surrounded by prose, or reject the request with a `400 Bad Request`.

lgtmaybe handles the first case for you: the parser strips fences and pulls the
JSON out of surrounding prose, so a gateway that ignores `response_format` still
produces a normal review.

A third case is common with LM Studio serving a "thinking" model (e.g.
qwen3.x): the server accepts `response_format`, but the schema-constrained
decoder returns empty content. lgtmaybe handles this too. It retries an empty
reply once with the schema sent as a forced tool call instead; if the model
answers empty under that as well, lgtmaybe stops sending a schema to that model
and the parser reads the findings from plain text. No flag needed.

When a gateway rejects `response_format` with a `400`, lgtmaybe recognises some
refusals that name the parameter and steps down by itself. If yours still fails,
turn structured output off so the request never carries the parameter. The
prompt still asks for JSON and the lenient parser still does its job:

```bash
lgtmaybe review \
  --provider openai-compatible \
  --model gemini-3.5-flash \
  --api-base https://api.myllm.com/v1 \
  --no-structured-output
```

Persist it as `structured_output: false` in `.lgtmaybe.yml`, or set the
Action's `structured_output` input to `false`.

[deepseek]: https://api-docs.deepseek.com/
[llamacpp]: https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp
[lmstudio]: https://lmstudio.ai/
[vllm]: https://docs.vllm.ai/
[ollama]: https://ollama.com/
[wf]: https://github.com/MattJColes/lgtmaybe/blob/main/examples/workflows/review-openai-compatible.yml

# Configure .lgtmaybe.yml

Put a `.lgtmaybe.yml` file at the root of your repository to set how lgtmaybe
reviews it. lgtmaybe reads the file from the directory it runs in, which is the
repo root for both the CLI and the GitHub Action. Pass `--config PATH` (or the
Action's `config_path` input) to read a different file; an explicit path must
exist.

The file holds non-secret settings only. API keys stay in the environment or
your CI secrets.

## Contents

- [Full Example](#full-example)
- [Field Reference](#field-reference)
  - [provider](#provider)
  - [model](#model)
  - [fallback_model](#fallback_model)
  - [min_severity](#min_severity)
  - [include_paths / exclude_paths](#include_paths-exclude_paths)
  - [max_files](#max_files)
  - [max_input_tokens](#max_input_tokens)
  - [preset](#preset)
  - [categories](#categories)
  - [context_lines](#context_lines)
  - [function_context](#function_context)
  - [timeout](#timeout)
  - [structured_output](#structured_output)
  - [reflect](#reflect)
  - [min_confidence](#min_confidence)
  - [mid_review_retrieval](#mid_review_retrieval)
  - [incremental](#incremental)
  - [static_analysis](#static_analysis)
  - [triage_model](#triage_model)
  - [auto_diagram](#auto_diagram)
  - [auto_describe](#auto_describe)
  - [high_impact](#high_impact)
  - [risk](#risk)
  - [pr_labels](#pr_labels)
  - [finding_rules](#finding_rules)
  - [summary_template](#summary_template)
  - [resolve_fixed](#resolve_fixed)
