<!-- Source: https://lgtmaybe.coles.codes/how-to/review-before-you-commit/ -->

# Review Before You Commit

lgtmaybe ships two hooks for the [pre-commit](https://pre-commit.com) framework,
so a local review runs from your Git hooks with no extra scripting:

| Hook id | Stage | Runs | Reviews |
|---|---|---|---|
| `lgtmaybe-pre-push` | `pre-push` | `lgtmaybe review` | Your branch's commits against the remote's primary branch |
| `lgtmaybe` | `pre-commit` | `lgtmaybe review --uncommitted` | The changes you are about to commit, against `HEAD` |

Both print findings exactly as `lgtmaybe review` does. Nothing is posted
anywhere.

## Contents

- [Before You Start](#before-you-start)
- [Add the Hook](#add-the-hook)
- [Block on Findings](#block-on-findings)
- [Review Every Commit Instead](#review-every-commit-instead)
- [Use a Keyless Cloud Provider](#use-a-keyless-cloud-provider)
- [Skip the Review Once](#skip-the-review-once)
- [See Also](#see-also)

## Before You Start

- **Each run calls your model.** A review is one or more model calls, so it
  takes time and, on a hosted provider, costs money every time the hook fires.
  That is why `pre-push` (one review per push) is the recommended stage rather
  than `pre-commit` (one review per commit). ollama keeps it local and free.
- **Credentials come from your environment.** The hook runs in your shell's
  environment, so export your provider's key (for example `OPENAI_API_KEY` or
  `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`) the same way you would for a manual
  `lgtmaybe review`. lgtmaybe never saves API keys in its config.
- **Pick the provider and model once.** Run `lgtmaybe config init` to save a
  default provider and model in your user config, or put them in the repo's
  [`.lgtmaybe.yml`](configure-lgtmaybe-yml.md), or pass them as hook `args`.
- **pre-commit 3.2.0 or later.** The hooks use the `pre-commit` and `pre-push`
  stage names, which arrived in that release.

pre-commit installs lgtmaybe into its own virtual environment from the tagged
source, so you do not need lgtmaybe installed separately for the hook. The
first run takes a minute or two while pre-commit builds that environment.

## Add the Hook

Add this to `.pre-commit-config.yaml` at the root of your repository. Pin `rev`
to a release tag that includes the hooks (v2.12.0 or later);
`pre-commit autoupdate` moves it to the latest release:

```yaml
repos:
  - repo: https://github.com/MattJColes/lgtmaybe
    rev: v2.12.0
    hooks:
      - id: lgtmaybe-pre-push
        args: [--provider, anthropic, --model, claude-sonnet-4-6, --fail-on, high]
```

Then install the Git hook for the `pre-push` stage:

```bash
pre-commit install --hook-type pre-push
```

The next `git push` reviews your branch first. To try it without pushing:

```bash
pre-commit run lgtmaybe-pre-push --hook-stage pre-push
```

Any `lgtmaybe review` flag works in `args`. For example, add `--base`,
`origin/develop` when your branch targets something other than the remote's
default branch, or `--min-severity`, `medium` to print less.

## Block on Findings

Without `--fail-on` the hook is advisory: it prints the review and lets the
push through. Both hooks set `verbose: true`, so the findings show even when
the hook passes.

With `--fail-on <severity>` (as in the example above), `lgtmaybe review` exits
with exit code 3 when any finding is at or above that severity, after printing
the findings, so pre-commit stops the push. A review that could not run at all
(for example, missing credentials or an unreachable model) exits 1, which also
stops the push; a usage error exits 2.

Only the command-line flag gates a local review. A `fail_on` set in
`.lgtmaybe.yml` is the GitHub Action's merge gate and never changes the exit
code of a local run, so configuring CI does not suddenly block your pushes.

## Review Every Commit Instead

To review each commit as you make it, use the `lgtmaybe` hook and install the
default hook type:

```yaml
repos:
  - repo: https://github.com/MattJColes/lgtmaybe
    rev: v2.12.0
    hooks:
      - id: lgtmaybe
```

```bash
pre-commit install
```

While hooks run, pre-commit sets your unstaged edits aside, so the review covers
what you have staged. Untracked files in the working tree are reviewed too.
Because this calls your model on every commit, prefer a local model (see
[Run locally with ollama](run-locally-with-ollama.md)) or the `pre-push` hook.

## Use a Keyless Cloud Provider

The hook installs the base package, which covers every API-key provider plus
ollama and OpenAI-compatible servers. For keyless Bedrock, Vertex or Azure, add
the cloud SDK the matching extra would install:

```yaml
      - id: lgtmaybe-pre-push
        args: [--provider, bedrock, --model, us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-6]
        additional_dependencies: [boto3]   # vertex: google-auth, azure: azure-identity
```

Your ambient credentials (`~/.aws`, `gcloud auth application-default login`,
`az login`) are used as they are for a manual run.

## Skip the Review Once

pre-commit's usual escape hatches apply:

```bash
SKIP=lgtmaybe-pre-push git push   # skip only this hook
git push --no-verify              # skip every pre-push hook
```

If you use [pre-commit.ci](https://pre-commit.ci), add the hook id to its
`skip` list: it has no model credentials, so the review cannot run there. Use
the [GitHub Action](use-as-github-action.md) to review pull requests in CI.

## See Also

- [Install the CLI](install-the-cli.md) - the same `lgtmaybe review` the hooks run
- [Fix findings with an AI agent](fix-findings-with-an-ai-agent.md) - turn local findings into corrections
- [Reduce review cost](reduce-review-cost.md) - make each run cheaper

<!-- Source: https://lgtmaybe.coles.codes/how-to/upload-findings-as-sarif/ -->

# Upload Findings as SARIF

`lgtmaybe review --format sarif` prints the findings as a
[SARIF 2.1.0](https://docs.oasis-open.org/sarif/sarif/v2.1.0/sarif-v2.1.0.html)
log instead of a listing. SARIF is the format GitHub code scanning ingests, and
most IDEs have a SARIF viewer, so the same findings can live next to your other
static-analysis alerts rather than in pull request comments.

## Write the Log

```bash
lgtmaybe review --provider openai --model gpt-5.5 --format sarif > lgtmaybe.sarif
```

stdout carries the SARIF log and nothing else. The token footer, the `--profile`
table, and the "results may be incomplete" notice all go to stderr, so the
redirect always captures a parseable file. Every other `review` option
(`--working`, `--base`, `--min-severity` and so on) works as usual.

## What the Log Contains

| SARIF field | Comes from |
|---|---|
| `tool.driver.rules` | One rule per review lens that raised a finding (`security`, `correctness`, ...), sorted |
| `results[].ruleId` | The finding's lens; `review` when it has none |
| `results[].level` | `critical` and `high` are `error`, `medium` is `warning`, `low` and `info` are `note` |
| `results[].message.text` | The finding's title, a blank line, then its body |
| `results[].locations` | The repo-relative file, plus `region.startLine` when the line is real |
| `results[].partialFingerprints` | `lgtmaybeFingerprint/v1` and `lgtmaybeIdentity/v1`, the same ids lgtmaybe hides in posted comments |
| `results[].properties` | `severity`, plus `confidence` (0 to 10) and `suggestion` when present |
| `invocations[].executionSuccessful` | `false` when a review lens failed, so a partial log never reads as clean |

A finding whose anchor matched no changed line, or one on the old (LEFT) side of
the diff, names its file without a line. Its line number would be a guess or
would point into the old file, and a wrong-line alert misleads more than a
file-level one. The suggested fix is free text rather than an exact replacement,
so it is kept in `properties.suggestion` instead of a SARIF `fixes` entry.

The output is deterministic: the same findings give the same bytes, so a re-run
uploads an identical log.

## Upload to GitHub Code Scanning

Code scanning must be available on the repository (public repositories, or
private ones with GitHub Code Security). This workflow reviews each pull request
from a branch in the same repository and uploads the log:

```yaml
name: lgtmaybe SARIF

on:
  pull_request:

permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  review:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: read
      security-events: write # upload-sarif
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
        with:
          fetch-depth: 0 # lgtmaybe diffs against the base branch
          persist-credentials: false
      - uses: astral-sh/setup-uv@v7
      - name: Review
        env:
          OPENAI_API_KEY: ${{ secrets.OPENAI_API_KEY }}
          BASE_REF: ${{ github.base_ref }}
        run: |
          uvx lgtmaybe review --provider openai --model gpt-5.5 \
            --base "origin/$BASE_REF" --format sarif > lgtmaybe.sarif
      - uses: github/codeql-action/upload-sarif@v4
        with:
          sarif_file: lgtmaybe.sarif
          category: lgtmaybe
```

`BASE_REF` goes through an environment variable rather than being expanded into
the script, which keeps workflow expressions out of the shell. `category` keeps
lgtmaybe's alerts separate from CodeQL or any other SARIF upload on the same
commit.

This runs on `pull_request` and checks out the pull request, which is fine for
branches in your own repository. A pull request from a fork gets no secrets on
`pull_request`, so the review step has no key. To review fork pull requests, use
the [GitHub Action](use-as-github-action.md) instead: it runs on
`pull_request_target`, reads the diff through the API, and never checks out PR
code.

## Open It in an IDE

Any SARIF viewer can open the file directly, for example the SARIF Viewer
extension for VS Code. Result paths are relative to `%SRCROOT%`; point the
viewer at your repository root when it asks.

## See Also

- [Install the CLI](install-the-cli.md)
- [Fix findings with an AI agent](fix-findings-with-an-ai-agent.md): the
  `--format agent` output
- [What gets reviewed](../explanation/what-gets-reviewed.md): every finding field

<!-- Source: https://lgtmaybe.coles.codes/how-to/use-from-a-coding-agent-over-mcp/ -->

# Use from a Coding Agent over MCP

`lgtmaybe mcp` runs a [Model Context Protocol](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/)
server on stdio. A coding agent such as Claude Code or Cursor connects to it and
reviews your local changes by calling a tool, instead of running
`lgtmaybe review` in a shell and parsing what it prints. The review is the same
one `lgtmaybe review` runs: the same engine, the same config files, the same
credentials. Nothing is posted anywhere.

## Contents

- [Install the MCP Extra](#install-the-mcp-extra)
- [Add It to Claude Code](#add-it-to-claude-code)
- [Add It to Another MCP Client](#add-it-to-another-mcp-client)
- [The Tools](#the-tools)
- [Credentials and Config](#credentials-and-config)
- [Troubleshooting](#troubleshooting)
- [See Also](#see-also)

## Install the MCP Extra

The MCP SDK is an optional extra, so a plain install stays small. Install it
with pip (or `uv tool install` / `pipx install`, which put `lgtmaybe` on your
`PATH` in an isolated environment):

```bash
pip install 'lgtmaybe[mcp]'
```

The Homebrew formula and the Windows executable do not include the extra; use
pip for `lgtmaybe mcp`. Without it the command exits with a message naming the
extra to install.

## Add It to Claude Code

From the repository you want reviewed, register the server with `claude mcp add`.
Everything after `--` is the command Claude Code runs; the `lgtmaybe mcp` flags
apply to every review the agent asks for:

```bash
claude mcp add lgtmaybe -- lgtmaybe mcp \
  --provider ollama \
  --model qwen3.6:27b \
  --api-base http://localhost:11434
```

Claude Code starts the server in the project directory, so the review sees that
repository. Add `--scope project` to write the entry to the repository's
`.mcp.json` and share it with your team. The entry stores the command and every
flag exactly as you typed them, so never pass `--api-key` to `claude mcp add` or
write it into `.mcp.json`: the key would sit in a file you commit. Supply API
keys through environment variables instead (see
[Credentials and Config](#credentials-and-config)).

Then ask the agent for a review in plain words, for example:

> Review my uncommitted changes with lgtmaybe and fix anything high severity.

## Add It to Another MCP Client

Most clients (Cursor, Windsurf, Claude Desktop and others) read an
`mcpServers` block from a JSON config file. Add an entry that runs
`lgtmaybe mcp`. Pass `-C` with the repository path when the client does not
start servers inside your project:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "lgtmaybe": {
      "command": "lgtmaybe",
      "args": [
        "mcp",
        "--provider", "openai",
        "--model", "gpt-5.5",
        "-C", "/path/to/your/repo"
      ]
    }
  }
}
```

If the client cannot find `lgtmaybe`, give the full path to the executable
(`which lgtmaybe` prints it) as `command`.

## The Tools

The server offers two tools. Both take the same optional arguments and run one
full review per call.

| Tool | Returns |
| --- | --- |
| `review_changes` | The findings as JSON, in the same shape as `lgtmaybe review --format json`, plus the `summary` line and `incomplete` (true when some review calls did not finish, so the findings may be partial). |
| `review_instructions` | The findings as plain-text correction instructions, the same text as `lgtmaybe review --format agent` except for the closing line, which tells the agent to call the `review_instructions` tool again (not to run `lgtmaybe review`) to confirm its fixes. |

| Argument | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `mode` | `branch` (default): committed branch changes against the base. `working`: branch commits plus uncommitted edits. `uncommitted`: only the uncommitted edits against `HEAD`. |
| `base` | The base ref to diff against, like `--base`. Defaults to the remote's primary branch. |
| `min_severity` | Drop findings below `info`, `low`, `medium`, `high` or `critical`. |
| `preset` | `fast` (five model calls) or `full` (one call per review category). |

A review that cannot run (not a Git repository, a missing credential, a provider
error) comes back as a tool error with the reason, so the agent sees what went
wrong rather than an empty result. The server keeps running for the next call.

Reviews run one at a time. A review makes several model calls, so it takes as
long as `lgtmaybe review` does; ask for one per change set rather than after
every edit.

## Credentials and Config

Config loads exactly as it does for `lgtmaybe review`: your user config
(`lgtmaybe config`), then the repository's `.lgtmaybe.yml`, then the flags on
`lgtmaybe mcp`, then the tool call's own arguments. The config files are read on
every call, so an edit to `.lgtmaybe.yml` applies without restarting the server.
A config file that does not parse stops the server at startup, where the client
shows the error.

API keys come from the environment, as they do for the CLI (`OPENAI_API_KEY`,
`ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` and so on; see the provider how-tos). The server inherits
the environment the client starts it with, so export the key in the shell you
start the client from. If your client starts servers without your shell
environment, set the key in the entry's `env` block instead, keeping in mind
that this stores it in the client's config file. lgtmaybe itself never writes a
key to disk. Keyless providers need no key at all: ollama, and Bedrock, Vertex
or Azure with ambient cloud credentials.

## Troubleshooting

- **The client says the server failed to start.** Run the same command in a
  terminal. A missing extra or a broken config prints its reason and exits.
  Otherwise the command waits silently for a client, which means it works.
- **The tool error says it is not a Git repository.** The server started outside
  your project. Add `-C /path/to/your/repo` to its arguments.
- **Where are the logs?** On stderr, which the client usually records in its MCP
  log. stdout carries only the protocol, so nothing lgtmaybe logs can corrupt it.

## See Also

- [Fix findings with an AI agent](fix-findings-with-an-ai-agent.md) - the same
  review-and-fix loop through files, without MCP
- [Configure .lgtmaybe.yml](configure-lgtmaybe-yml.md) - every option a review reads
- [Install the CLI](install-the-cli.md) - pip, Homebrew and WinGet installs

<!-- Source: https://lgtmaybe.coles.codes/how-to/reduce-review-cost/ -->

# Reduce Review Cost

A review makes several model calls per diff batch, and every call pays for its
input even when prompt caching discounts it. Large diffs create more batches,
so cost on a hosted provider can rise quickly.

This guide shows you how to measure that cost and lower it while keeping the
findings you need.

> Deciding **who** can trigger a review is a related but separate question. See
> [Trust and Cost](../explanation/trust-and-cost.md). Every setting below is
> documented field by field in the [configuration reference](../reference/config.md).

## Contents

- [First, Measure](#first-measure)
- [Where the Tokens Go](#where-the-tokens-go)
- [The Levers, in Order of Payoff](#the-levers-in-order-of-payoff)
- [Put a Hard Ceiling on It](#put-a-hard-ceiling-on-it)
- [If a Call Runs Past `max_tokens`](#if-a-call-runs-past-max_tokens)
- [If One Lens Floods the Review](#if-one-lens-floods-the-review)
- [What Costs More, on Purpose](#what-costs-more-on-purpose)
- [What Isn't Worth Changing](#what-isnt-worth-changing)

## First, Measure

Do not tune blind. Run once with `--profile`:

```bash
lgtmaybe review --profile
```

The table ends with the meter:

```
tokens: 158,076 billable (154,200 in / 3,876 out) across 12 calls
```

Every local review prints this line to stderr even without `--profile`, so the
meter is always in view. Redirect with `2>/dev/null` if you want it gone.

When litellm's pricing map knows the model, a second line follows:

```
estimated cost: $0.5207 (litellm pricing map)
```

It is an estimate from a price list that can lag a brand-new model, so a
missing line means "unpriced", not "free". When only some calls could be
priced, the line says how many (`; 9 of 12 calls priced`) rather than passing a
partial total off as the sum. Cache reads are billed at their discount, so a
run with a warm prefix shows it.

`in` usually dwarfs `out` because every review call carries diff content. The
per-call table shows which lens and batch each call belongs to, so you can see
whether the cost comes from call count, batch count, or one large file.

On a reasoning model, read the table's `think_tok` column next to `out_tok`. It
is how much of the output budget went on thought before the model wrote a
single finding, and a summary line totals it:

```
reasoning: 41,300 of 47,900 output tokens (86%)
```

The line appears only when a route reports the breakdown. Its absence means
"not reported", not "no thinking". A high share explains a lens that ran for a
minute and returned three findings, and it is the number to check before
[raising `max_tokens`](#if-a-call-runs-past-max_tokens).

In the GitHub Action, set `profile: true` and the same breakdown lands in the
job log. Every provider call also emits a structured `provider call` log line
with its own token counts, so you can total a run without the table.

## Where the Tokens Go

For one review:

```
input tokens  ≈  batches × calls per batch × (diff + context padding + hints)
```

- **Calls per batch.** The `fast` preset (the default) makes four core calls
  per batch. `full` makes one per built-in category, up to nine. A matching
  committed spec adds its own call. This is the biggest multiplier in the
  formula.
- **Batches.** A diff larger than `max_input_tokens` is split, and each batch
  pays the full lens fan-out again. The default is 100k, fitted down to the
  model's context window when that is known (litellm's model map for hosted
  models, `num_ctx` for ollama, less the output ceiling). A value you set is
  used as-is.
- **Reflection.** One more pass over the findings.
- **Triage.** One extra cheap call when enabled.
- **The change overview** (`auto_diagram`, on by default). Up to three extra
  calls per push: the description (`auto_describe`), High Impact Areas
  (`high_impact`), and the diagrams. Each section opts out on its own;
  `auto_diagram: false` drops all three.
- **Mid-review retrieval.** Off by default. When on, it adds up to one more
  call per (batch, lens). See [What Costs More, on Purpose](#what-costs-more-on-purpose).

Two settings look expensive but are not: `max_concurrency` only changes how
many calls run at once, never how many there are, and `temperature` costs
nothing.

## The Levers, in Order of Payoff

### 1. Turn On Triage

A cheap model reads the per-file diffs first and drops files that plainly do
not need a review. The expensive model only sees the survivors, riskiest
first.

```yaml
triage_model: claude-haiku-4-5
```

This is usually the biggest single win on a repo with lots of low-substance
churn (generated files, config bumps, test fixtures). It cannot quietly hide a
problem: a deterministic security floor (auth and crypto paths, migrations,
IaC, CI workflows, dependency manifests, static-analysis hits, large hunks)
always escalates past triage, any triage failure reviews everything, and
skipped files are named in the summary. `triage_model`, `model` and
`reflect_model` share one provider and one set of credentials.

### 2. Let Deterministic Tools Do the Deterministic Work

Findings a linter can prove do not need a language model:

```bash
pip install 'lgtmaybe[static-analysis]'
```

```yaml
static_analysis:
  enabled: true
```

Installed tools run over the changed files at no token cost. The interpretive
ones (ruff, bandit, mypy, and semgrep with local rules) feed their findings to
the lenses as hints to confirm or discard, which grounds the model and tends to
cut low-value findings as well as spend. The deterministic ones (gitleaks,
zizmor, ast-grep with your own rules, osv-scanner) post their findings
directly with no model call. A tool that is not installed is skipped.

### 3. Check Prompt Caching Is Working

Prompt caching is always on. When it works, it takes most of the sting out of
the lens multiplier: lenses 2..N read the shared system preamble and diff from
cache instead of paying full input price for them.

Check the profile's cache line:

```
cache: 412000 tokens read / 38000 created across 12 calls
```

Reads climbing across a run means caching is working. Reads stuck near zero
means you are paying full price for every lens. lgtmaybe sets an explicit
cache breakpoint on the routes that take one (anthropic, bedrock Claude and
Nova, vertex, zai, and openrouter's Claude, Gemini and GLM families). OpenAI,
Azure and DeepSeek cache identical prefixes server-side with no marker. A route
with neither gets no discount, which is a strong argument for picking one that
has it.

### 4. Narrow the Lenses

An explicit `categories` list runs exactly those lenses, one call each, per
batch:

```yaml
categories: [security, correctness]
```

That is two calls per batch instead of the default four. Keep the list short:
an explicit list turns off the `fast` preset's grouping, so listing six
categories costs six calls, not four.

Otherwise keep the default `fast` preset. `preset: full` more than doubles the
call count (up to nine calls per batch instead of four) for a modest recall
gain.

### 5. Review Less

```yaml
exclude_paths: ["**/migrations/**", "**/*.generated.ts"]
max_files: 25
max_file_diff_lines: 1000
```

Generated, vendored and binary files are already skipped, and a single file
whose patch exceeds `max_file_diff_lines` (default 2000) is dropped and named
in the summary. Path filters cut the rest before any model call, so they are
pure saving.

### 6. Let Re-runs Be Incremental

On the Action's `synchronize` event, a re-run reviews only the commits since
the last reviewed SHA rather than the whole PR. That is the default, so leave
`incremental` unset. Comment `/review full` when you want everything
re-reviewed.

The `gitlab-ci` command does the same on every merge request pipeline after
the first. To re-review everything there, run the pipeline with
`LGTMAYBE_INCREMENTAL=false`.

Locally there is no watermark: every `lgtmaybe review` re-reviews the whole
branch at full price. If you are iterating, review only what you just changed:

```bash
lgtmaybe review --uncommitted    # working-tree edits vs HEAD
```

### 7. Right-Size the Model

A smaller primary model with a stronger fallback cuts expected cost when the
primary usually finishes its calls. A healthy call never reaches the fallback.
A failed call still spends the primary model's attempts before trying the
second model, so this does not reduce worst-case cost.

```yaml
provider: openrouter
model: google/gemini-3.7-flash
fallback_model: qwen/qwen3.8-max
```

Both models use the same configured provider and credentials. See
[`fallback_model`](configure-lgtmaybe-yml.md#fallback_model) for the recovery
order, failure behaviour, and reporting.

If cost matters more than latency, ollama runs locally for free:

```bash
lgtmaybe review --provider ollama --model qwen2.5-coder:14b
```

## Put a Hard Ceiling on It

Tuning changes the expected cost. A ceiling bounds the worst case.

```yaml
max_review_tokens: 300000
```

Once a run's billable tokens (input plus output across every model call) reach
the ceiling, no further calls are dispatched. In-flight calls finish, their
findings post, and the summary says that the budget stopped the run and how
many calls were skipped. It never turns a failure into a silent `LGTM`.

It is off by default on purpose. Spend scales with diff size, lens count and
batch count, so any figure that protects a small repo would silently truncate a
large one's review. Read a real run's total with `--profile` first, then set
the ceiling comfortably above it. It is a runaway guard, not a tuning knob.

## If a Call Runs Past `max_tokens`

`max_tokens` caps what one call may write. A lens that hits it comes back cut
off mid-JSON, and lowering it to save money is the usual way to get here.

On `ollama`, `openai-compatible` and `openrouter`, a default ceiling of 16384
tokens per call applies, so you can get here without setting anything. It
exists because a model under structured output can fail to terminate and keep
decoding until the timeout stops it half an hour later. The first-party APIs
get no default ceiling.

You do not have to do anything. lgtmaybe treats an over-ceiling call the same
way as one that outruns its wall clock: the batch was more than one call could
cover, so it is halved and the pieces are reviewed separately, each with a
fresh ceiling. Whatever the model finished writing before the cut is kept, so
nothing already paid for is thrown away. The summary says a batch was shrunk
and, because part of a lens is not a whole lens, that results may be
incomplete.

That recovery costs up to twice the calls for the affected batch. The pieces
run concurrently, so on the clock it costs about one extra call. It is bounded
to one split level: a piece that still runs past the ceiling is not split
again. If the pieces still fail and you set `fallback_model`, the batch's lens
is re-run once on the fallback as a last resort.

When you see splits often, the fix is usually `max_tokens`, not the diff:

```yaml
max_tokens: 32768
```

A reasoning model spends the same budget on thinking before it writes a single
finding, which is how a fifteen-line diff can truncate. The failure names the
reasoning tokens where the provider reports them. When they account for
essentially the whole ceiling, lgtmaybe does not split the batch, because
smaller pieces would each spend the same ceiling on thought. Instead it re-runs
the lens once at one lower `reasoning_effort` level, then once with reasoning
off if that also truncates, and only then on `fallback_model`.

You do not have to wait for a truncation to see this coming. `--profile`
reports the same split on calls that succeeded (`think_tok` and the
`reasoning:` total). A truncated call cannot tell you that: it spent reasoning
plus findings ≥ `max_tokens` by definition, so it says nothing about the
healthy calls beside it.

Two more numbers answer the headroom question directly:

- the **`think_%`** column: that call's thinking as a share of the
  `max_tokens` ceiling it ran under;
- a **`largest reasoning share:`** line under the table, naming the single
  call closest to the ceiling and its lens.

An 8,192-token cap whose worst lens reports 50% has real headroom. One
reporting 95% is a truncation that has not happened yet, and the aggregate
`reasoning:` line will not show it, because one runaway hides inside an
average.

A route that reports no breakdown shows `-` in both columns and prints no
`largest` line. That is not zero. The route never said, so there is nothing to
conclude either way.

### When the Cap Is Not the Lever

If `think_tok` is most of `out_tok`, raising `max_tokens` will not fix the
truncation, because the reasoning expands into the new headroom. Bound the
thinking instead:

```yaml
reasoning_effort: low   # none | minimal | low | medium | high | xhigh | default
```

This is measured. On lgtmaybe's own dogfood review, 5 of 9 lens calls spent
32,000-35,000 reasoning tokens (at or above the whole 32,768 `max_tokens`
ceiling) before writing a single finding. The one large call that completed
wrote roughly 733 tokens of findings after 28,909 tokens of thought. Raising
the cap from 16k to 32k had not helped; it only gave the model more room to
think.

Unset sends nothing, so a route without a reasoning channel is unaffected.

Some models treat effort as a switch rather than a dial. GLM 5.3 through
OpenRouter spent a 12,288-token ceiling on thought at `low` and again at
`minimal`, in 10 retries of 11; only `none` changed it. lgtmaybe's recovery
ladder takes that step for you (one level down, then reasoning off, then the
fallback model), but on such a model configuring `none` saves the two failed
calls that come first.

#### Cheaper Is Not Better Value

Bounding thinking fixes a reasoning-bound truncation. It is not a free saving,
and the direction that saves tokens is not the direction that finds bugs.
Measured on lgtmaybe's own repo, two runs per setting on the same diff:

| | `low` | `medium` |
|---|---|---|
| findings | 2, 2 | 5, 4 |
| false positives | 0, 1 | 0, 0 |
| output tokens | ~4-5k | ~14k |
| **total billable** | 180,704 | 187,191 |

`medium` roughly triples output tokens and still costs only about 4% more in
total, because a review is overwhelmingly input: the diff, the context, the
system prompt. Weighting output at 4× its input price puts it nearer 20%.
Either way, nothing like the 3× the output column suggests.

What `medium` bought was a bug in lgtmaybe's own retry backoff that `low` missed
in both runs, and `low` produced the only false positive of the four. Treat
`reasoning_effort` as a quality dial that moves cost a little, not a cost dial
that moves quality. Turn it down when reasoning is eating your `max_tokens`
ceiling, not to save money.

#### On OpenRouter, Check the Log Line

litellm forwards `reasoning_effort` to OpenRouter only for models its
capability map already flags as reasoning-capable, and the newest models are
often missing from it. For those, lgtmaybe sends the budget in OpenRouter's own
top-level `reasoning` object, so the setting is enforced either way.

More generally, any configured parameter the resolved model will not accept is
named once at startup rather than dropped in silence:

```
configured params are not supported by this model and will be ignored
```

If that line names a setting you meant to apply, the setting is not in force.
Pick a different model or drop the setting. `reasoning_effort: default` on
OpenRouter is one real case: it is in litellm's vocabulary but not in
OpenRouter's `reasoning.effort` enum (`none`, `minimal`, `low`, `medium`,
`high`, `xhigh`), so it is reported rather than quietly mapped to a nearby
level.

## If One Lens Floods the Review

A lens can stay within its token budget and still return far too many findings
by restating one claim against every line it can see. On a benchmark diff with
nothing wrong in it, a single lens returned 319 of a review's 323 findings, each
on a different line. Location dedupe does not collapse them, because no two
share a line.

So one `(batch, lens)` call contributes at most 50 findings by default. When
the bound fires, the highest-severity findings are kept and the summary names
the lens and how many were dropped:

```
⚠️ Bounded a lens to the top 50 findings by severity: `intent` (269 dropped). A lens
returning many more findings than this is usually restating one claim across many
lines. Raise max_findings_per_lens to keep them all.
```

The notice usually points to a problem with the model, not a bound set too
low. A lens returning hundreds of findings is generating badly, and a higher
bound admits more of the same. Raise it only when a genuinely large diff is
losing real findings:

```yaml
max_findings_per_lens: 100   # 0 disables the bound entirely
```

An ordinary lens returns a handful of findings and never reaches the bound.

## What Costs More, on Purpose

One setting runs the other way: `mid_review_retrieval` buys findings with
tokens. Know the price before you turn it on.

```yaml
mid_review_retrieval: true   # default false
```

Normally a lens that cannot decide without reading code outside the diff is told
to hedge the claim or drop it, so a bug whose evidence sits one file away is
never reported. With this on, the lens may instead name the files or symbols it
needs. lgtmaybe fetches them read-only and re-runs that one lens with them.

The worst case is one extra model call per (batch, lens), each also carrying
the fetched file text. On the default four-lens preset over three batches, that
is up to twelve extra calls: the multiplier in the formula above, doubled. In
practice only the lenses that defer pay it, and the fetch is capped at five
files within a quarter of `max_input_tokens`, but budget for the worst case.

To keep the bill in check:

- Pair it with `max_review_tokens`, so the worst case is bounded rather than
  merely unlikely. A deferral that arrives past the ceiling is skipped and
  reported.
- Fetched text rides the lens's own block, so a deferral never invalidates the
  shared cached prefix that sibling lenses read.
- Turn on `triage_model` first, so fewer files reach the lenses that might
  defer.

Measure rather than assume: run `python -m evals.run` with and without
`--mid-review-retrieval` against your model and compare recall to the token
total.

## What Isn't Worth Changing

**`context_lines`.** The obvious saving is not there. Measured across four real
multi-file commits in this repository, the padding around each hunk costs about
41% over sending no context at all, but only about 17% between
`context_lines: 5` and the default `20`. Hunks with overlapping windows merge,
and the reach to the enclosing definition does most of the useful widening
either way:

| `context_lines` | 0 | 5 | 10 | 20 (default) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| diff payload tokens | 28,316 | 34,265 | 36,072 | 40,041 |
| vs. no context | 1.00× | 1.21× | 1.27× | 1.41× |

Saving roughly a seventh of your input tokens by hiding the function a change
sits in is a bad trade. That context keeps findings anchored and cuts false
positives. Turn the multiplier down (fewer lenses, triage, caching) before you
turn the context down.

---

<!-- Source: https://lgtmaybe.coles.codes/how-to/releasing/ -->

# Releasing lgtmaybe (maintainers)

Releases are automated by **release-please**
(`.github/workflows/release-please.yml`). It reads the **conventional commits**
merged to `main` and keeps a Release PR open that bumps the version and
regenerates `CHANGELOG.md`. **Merging that PR** is the release: release-please
creates the `lgtmaybe-vX.Y.Z` tag and the GitHub release, and the same run then
publishes everywhere:

- **PyPI**, through trusted publishing (OIDC) in an inline job.
- **GHCR image and Action tags**, through the reusable
  `.github/workflows/release.yml` using the built-in `GITHUB_TOKEN`. It pushes
  a multi-arch (amd64, arm64) image tagged `X.Y.Z`, `vX` (currently `v2`), and
  `latest`, and moves the git tags `vX.Y.Z`, `vX`, and `lgtmaybe-vX` to the
  release commit so workflows can use `MattJColes/lgtmaybe@v2`.
- **Homebrew**, through `.github/workflows/homebrew.yml`, after the PyPI job
  succeeds (described below).
- **Windows**, through `.github/workflows/windows-exe.yml`, which builds and
  smoke-tests a portable executable and attaches it to the release, then
  `.github/workflows/winget.yml`, which submits that asset to winget. The
  winget job waits for the executable job. Both workflows can be dispatched by
  hand for recovery.

PyPI and GHCR need no publish tokens in secrets. Homebrew and winget each need
one PAT, set up below.

Commit messages must follow the conventional-commit format.
`.github/workflows/commitlint.yml` enforces it on PRs so release-please can
work out the next version.

## Contents

- [The Homebrew formula](#the-homebrew-formula)
- [One-time setup](#one-time-setup)
- [Each release](#each-release)
- [Rotate the public App private key](#rotate-the-public-app-private-key)
- [Before going public](#before-going-public)

## The Homebrew Formula

`homebrew.yml` regenerates the formula in the tap repo
(`MattJColes/homebrew-tap`, which is the tap `MattJColes/tap`) so
`brew install MattJColes/tap/lgtmaybe` tracks the latest version.
`scripts/update-homebrew-formula.sh` writes a small formula that creates a venv
and `pip install`s lgtmaybe and its dependencies from **PyPI wheels**, with no
per-dependency `resource` stanzas. litellm's dependency tree includes Rust
sdists (tokenizers, hf-xet) that can't build in Homebrew's sandbox, so building
from source is a dead end. The formula declares **`preserve_rpath`** so
Homebrew keeps the wheels' `@rpath` extension-dylib ids instead of failing to
rewrite them ("Failed to fix install linkage"). It is a plain source formula
with no bottle, so it installs on any architecture and macOS version.

The workflow:

- Is **called** by `release-please.yml` (`workflow_call`) once the PyPI publish
  succeeds, because GitHub does not deliver a `release: published` event for a
  release cut with the built-in `GITHUB_TOKEN` (it suppresses downstream
  triggers to prevent recursion). It also runs on `release: published` for a
  release a human cuts, on a daily `schedule`, and on a manual
  `workflow_dispatch` (with an optional `force` to re-publish the same
  version).
- **Installs the regenerated formula in CI before committing it.** A real
  `brew trust` + `brew install` gates the push, so a formula that doesn't
  install is never published. The gate trusts the tap rather than setting
  `HOMEBREW_NO_REQUIRE_TAP_TRUST`, so it exercises the same steps the install
  guide gives users.

A new version reaches the tap within minutes of release. There is no PyPI
cooldown to wait out, because `brew update-python-resources` (which imposes
one) isn't used.

## One-Time Setup

- On PyPI, add a **trusted publisher** for this repo: workflow
  **`release-please.yml`**, environment `pypi`. There is no `PYPI_TOKEN`
  secret; auth is via OIDC. The publish job is inline in that workflow on
  purpose, because PyPI trusted publishing requires the OIDC `job_workflow_ref`
  to equal the top-level workflow.
- Create the repo **environment** named `pypi` (Settings → Environments).
- After the first release, set the **GHCR package visibility to public** so
  consumers can `docker pull` the image (Packages → lgtmaybe → Package settings).
- First release only: from the GitHub release page, tick **"Publish this Action
  to the GitHub Marketplace"**, accept the terms, and pick the categories
  `code-review` and `continuous-integration`.
- **Homebrew tap:** create the repo **`MattJColes/homebrew-tap`** with a
  `Formula/` directory. It can start empty; the workflow writes the formula.
  Homebrew strips the `homebrew-` prefix, so that repo is the tap
  `MattJColes/tap` and the formula inside it is `MattJColes/tap/lgtmaybe`. Name
  the repo `homebrew-tap`, not `homebrew-lgtmaybe`, or the formula reads as
  `MattJColes/lgtmaybe/lgtmaybe`. Add a repo secret **`HOMEBREW_TAP_TOKEN`** to
  *this* repo: a fine-grained PAT with `contents: write` on the tap repo (the
  default `GITHUB_TOKEN` cannot push to another repository). To seed or verify
  the formula by hand on a Mac, run
  `scripts/update-homebrew-formula.sh <version> path/to/homebrew-tap/Formula/lgtmaybe.rb`.
- **winget:** fork [`microsoft/winget-pkgs`](https://github.com/microsoft/winget-pkgs).
  Create a classic GitHub PAT with the `public_repo` **and `workflow`** scopes
  and add it to this repo as **`WINGET_TOKEN`**. `wingetcreate` syncs the fork
  with upstream before it opens each PR, and `microsoft/winget-pkgs` often
  changes files under `.github/workflows/`. GitHub refuses a fork sync that
  brings in workflow-file changes unless the token has the `workflow` scope, so
  with `public_repo` alone the submission fails on almost every release.
- **First winget release:** build and upload the Windows asset, then run
  `wingetcreate new <asset-url>` by hand with package id `MattJColes.lgtmaybe`,
  installer type `portable`, command alias `lgtmaybe`, and MIT licence
  metadata. Microsoft moderates a new package before it is published, which can
  take days or weeks. Until that first manifest is accepted, the release job
  warns and skips the winget update rather than failing the other release
  artefacts. After that, the workflow runs `wingetcreate update` for every
  new version.

## Each Release

1. Merge feature/fix PRs to `main` using conventional-commit messages
   (`feat:`, `fix:`, `feat!:` / `BREAKING CHANGE:` for a major bump).
2. release-please opens or updates the **Release PR** automatically. Review the
   proposed version + changelog, then **merge it** to publish. Once the release
   is cut, the `contributors` job appends a **Contributors** section to the
   GitHub release, naming the human authors of its pull requests and welcoming
   first-time contributors (`scripts/release_contributors.py`, fed by GitHub's
   generate-notes API; bots are left out). `CHANGELOG.md` is not touched, and
   the merge also republishes the docs, so the homepage's What's New list
   picks up the release.
3. To (re)publish an existing tag to PyPI without a new release, run the
   `release-please` workflow via **workflow_dispatch** with the tag name (for
   example `lgtmaybe-v2.11.1`). To rebuild the GHCR image and move the Action
   tags for an existing tag, dispatch `release` the same way.
4. If Windows publication needs recovery, dispatch `windows-exe` for the tag
   (set `force` to replace an existing asset), then dispatch `winget` once the
   release asset is visible.
5. If the `winget` job fails with "The forked repository could not be synced
   with the upstream commits", sync `MattJColes/winget-pkgs` with upstream
   (**Sync fork** on its `master`, or
   `gh api -X POST repos/MattJColes/winget-pkgs/merge-upstream -f branch=master`),
   then dispatch `winget` again with the version. If it keeps recurring, check
   that `WINGET_TOKEN` still carries the `workflow` scope.

## Rotate the Public App Private Key

Rotate the public `lgtmaybe` GitHub App key quarterly, whenever maintainer access
changes, and immediately after any suspected exposure. Keep the old key active
until the replacement has passed a brokered smoke test so rotation does not
interrupt reviews.

1. In the GitHub App settings, generate a new private key. Do not delete the old
   key yet.
2. From the directory containing the downloaded PEM, replace the retained
   Secrets Manager value without printing the key:

    ```bash
    aws secretsmanager put-secret-value \
      --secret-id lgtmaybe/github-app/private-key \
      --secret-string file://lgtmaybe.private-key.pem \
      --region ap-southeast-2
    ```

3. Refresh the Lambda configuration so every execution environment drops its
   cached copy of the old key:

    ```bash
    FUNCTION_NAME="$(
      aws cloudformation describe-stack-resources \
        --stack-name LgtmaybeGithubAppIdentity \
        --region ap-southeast-2 \
        --query "StackResources[?ResourceType=='AWS::Lambda::Function'].PhysicalResourceId | [0]" \
        --output text
    )"
    aws lambda update-function-configuration \
      --function-name "$FUNCTION_NAME" \
      --description "GitHub App key rotated $(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)" \
      --region ap-southeast-2
    aws lambda wait function-updated-v2 \
      --function-name "$FUNCTION_NAME" \
      --region ap-southeast-2
    ```

4. Run a brokered dogfood review and confirm GitHub attributes it to
   `lgtmaybe[bot]`.
5. Delete the old key in the GitHub App settings, then delete the downloaded PEM
   from the maintainer machine. Never paste the PEM into a command argument,
   issue, workflow log, or repository file.

If the smoke test fails, leave the old GitHub key active, put its PEM back into
the same Secrets Manager secret, refresh the Lambda configuration again, and
investigate before retrying.

## Before Going Public

- Dogfood lgtmaybe on its own PRs so the README example is real.
- Re-check the least-privilege IAM/WIF scopes (see the
  [Bedrock](./review-with-bedrock-oidc.md) and [Vertex](./review-with-vertex-wif.md)
  guides) before the repo goes public.

---

<!-- Source: https://lgtmaybe.coles.codes/how-to/write-docs/ -->

# Write the Docs

These docs are for every engineer, including one who has never used lgtmaybe
and is new to code review tools. Write so that the reader can follow along the
first time, without a second tab open to look things up.

## The Reader

Picture an engineer who knows how to use git and a terminal, but not this
project. They do not know our words for things yet. They want to get something
working, then understand why it works.

## How to Write

- **Put one idea in each paragraph.** If a paragraph needs a second idea, it
  needs a second paragraph.
- **Keep sentences short.** Aim for under 25 words. Split a sentence that has
  more than one "and", "which" or "because" in it.
- **Explain a term the first time you use it,** or link it to the
  [glossary](../reference/glossary.md). Project words such as
  "[lens](../reference/glossary.md#lens)",
  "[preset](../reference/glossary.md#preset)" and
  "[watermark](../reference/glossary.md#watermark)" must link to their glossary
  entry on every page that uses them.
- **Show before you explain.** Give the command or the config first, then say
  what it does and why.
- **Use the active voice.** Write "lgtmaybe posts a comment", not "a comment is
  posted".
- **Use a list for anything that is a list.** Three or more items in a sentence
  usually read better as bullets.
- **Keep facts exact.** Never change a config key, a default value, a command or
  a code example to make a sentence shorter. Shorter wording, never fewer facts.
- **Say what the reader will see.** "The run fails with a message naming the
  missing key" beats "an error occurs".

## House Style

- Headings use Title Case.
- Spelling is Australian English: "behaviour", "colour", "organise",
  "artefact".
- Write lgtmaybe and ollama in lowercase, even at the start of a sentence.
- Use " - " or a full stop, never an em dash.
- Skip filler such as "it's worth noting", "simply" and "just". Skip "not only X
  but also Y" and lists of three padded to sound complete.
- Do not end a section by restating what it said.

## What the Checks Enforce

`tests/docs/test_readability.py` reads each page's prose (not its code, tables
or headings) and fails when a page has:

- an average sentence over 18 words;
- any sentence over 35 words;
- an em dash;
- a key project term with no link to its glossary entry.

Run the checker yourself to see every problem on a page, with the sentence that
caused it:

```bash
uv run python scripts/doc_readability.py docs/how-to/your-page.md
```

Run it with no arguments for a summary of every page. Pages that do not pass yet
are listed in `NOT_YET_PASSING` in the test. That list can only shrink: when you
fix a page, the test fails until you take it off the list.

## Glossary and Tooltips

- Add a term to the [glossary](../reference/glossary.md) when a page needs it
  and it is not there yet. Keep the entry to two or three short sentences, and
  link to the page where the term matters.
- Acronyms such as OIDC and SARIF also get a hover tooltip on every page. Add
  one line to `includes/abbreviations.md`, and give it a glossary entry too.

## Before You Open a Pull Request

1. Run `uv run python docs/generate_llms_txt.py` so `docs/llms.txt` and
   `docs/llms-full.txt` match the pages.
2. Run `uv run --group docs mkdocs build --strict`. It also fails on a link to a
   heading that no longer exists.
3. Run `uv run pytest tests/docs -q`.

---

## Enums

### Provider

LLM backend selected by `--provider`. Cloud providers (`bedrock`, `vertex`, `azure`) use ambient credentials — `azure` also needs the resource endpoint (`--api-base`) and accepts a key as an alternative. `openai-compatible` points at any server speaking the OpenAI `/v1` wire format (DeepSeek, llama.cpp, LM Studio, vLLM) via `--api-base`; the key is optional so keyless local servers work.

- `anthropic`
- `azure`
- `bedrock`
- `ollama`
- `openai`
- `openai-compatible`
- `openrouter`
- `vertex`
- `zai`

### Severity

Finding severity, ordered low to high. Use `min_severity` in config to suppress findings below a threshold.

- `critical`
- `high`
- `info`
- `low`
- `medium`

## ReviewFinding

The structured output the model must return for each inline comment. All fields are validated by pydantic before anything is posted.

| Field | Type | Required | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `anchor` | string / null | No | `null` | Anchor |
| `anchored` | boolean | No | `True` | Anchored |
| `body` | string | Yes | — | Body |
| `broad` | boolean | No | `False` | Broad |
| `category` | string / null | No | `null` | Category |
| `confidence` | integer / null | No | `null` | Confidence |
| `failure_scenario` | string / null | No | `null` | Failure Scenario |
| `line` | integer | Yes | — | Line |
| `path` | string | Yes | — | Path |
| `severity` | `critical` / `high` / `info` / `low` / `medium` | Yes | — |  |
| `side` | string | No | `RIGHT` | Side |
| `suggestion` | string / null | No | `null` | Suggestion |
| `title` | string | Yes | — | Title |

| `input_tokens` | integer | Yes | — | Input Tokens |
| `model` | string / null | No | `null` | Model |

| `output_tokens` | integer | Yes | — | Output Tokens |
| `reasoning_tokens` | integer / null | No | `null` | Reasoning Tokens |
| `text` | string | Yes | — | Text |

## PRContext

Everything the engine needs about a pull request. Fetched via the GitHub REST API — PR code is never checked out.

| `repo` | string | Yes | — | Repo |
| `risk` | RiskAssessment / null | No | `null` |  |

| `title` | string | No | `` | Title |
